assessments.support: Diagnosis source/instrument is never stated; labels appear to be taken directly from ABIDE group assignment ('Each image was manually labelled and assigned a group') with no mention of ADOS/ADI-R or inclusion/exclusion criteria beyond 'resources and age'.

No preprocessing pipeline (e.g. CPAC/DPARSF), connectivity feature extraction, or atlas/parcellation is described; the paper refers only to 'images' and 'heat maps' fed to CNN/transfer-learning models with no stated derivation from raw rs-fMRI.
Outcome is binary ASD vs control classification, but how group labels were sourced/validated is not reported.

No train/test split ratio, cross-validation scheme, or held-out evaluation is reported for the authors' own experiments; results are reported per 'resource' (site) as separate subsets rather than leave-site-out; no measure of uncertainty (CI) is given around the single reported accuracy figures.

risk_of_bias.summary: Predictive classification study with no reported preprocessing/atlas, no reported train/test or cross-validation protocol, no leakage control statement, and no diagnosis-source documentation; accuracy figures are reported as single point estimates without uncertainty.

evidence_spans.text:
The secondary cohort was a subset of the ABIDE database
consisting of 58 HFASD (25.4[7.8] years, 37.9% female) and 51 typically developing controls (24.4[6.7] years, 39.2%
female).
evidence_spans.claim: The secondary (ABIDE) cohort consisted of 58 high-functioning ASD and 51 typically developing controls.

evidence_spans.text:
To validate our ﬁndings in a separate cohort, we iden-
tiﬁed 58 ASD and 51 TD individuals from ABIDE mat-
ched to the HFASD cohort by age, sex, and IQ (Table 2).
The selection process is detailed in Supplemental Infor-
mation.
evidence_spans.claim: 58 ASD and 51 TD individuals were identified from ABIDE, matched to the primary HFASD cohort by age, sex and IQ.

evidence_spans.text:
Func-
tional data from both the HFASD and ABIDE cohorts
were preprocessed identically using fMRIPrep v1.3.152, a
pipeline that uses a combination of tools from existing
neuroimaging software packages.
evidence_spans.claim: ABIDE (and HFASD) functional data were preprocessed identically using the fMRIPrep v1.3.1 pipeline.

evidence_spans.text:
In the ABIDE cohort, group-mean FD was
0.124 for ASD and 0.123 for TD (two sample t-test p =
0.8679).
evidence_spans.claim: Group-mean framewise displacement in the ABIDE cohort was 0.124 (ASD) and 0.123 (TD), not significantly different.

evidence_spans.text:
Frames that exhibited an FD of over 0.5 mm were
censored from the timeseries, as well as one before and
two after the offending frame.
evidence_spans.claim: Frames with FD over 0.5 mm (plus one before and two after) were censored (scrubbed) from the timeseries.

evidence_spans.text:
Participants with <80% of
their TRs retained after motion scrubbing were removed
from the analysis. As a result, a total of 20 TD participants
and 23 ASD participants were analyzed from the HFASD
cohort (Table 1). From ABIDE, 51 TD participants and 58
ASD participants were analyzed (Table 2).
evidence_spans.claim: Participants retaining under 80% of TRs after motion scrubbing were excluded, leaving 51 TD and 58 ASD from ABIDE.

evidence_spans.text:
To account for potential con-
founding effects from differences in scan acquisition
parameters, we included site as a covariate in our ABIDE
GLM analysis as one-hot encoded variables.
evidence_spans.claim: Site was included as a one-hot-encoded covariate in the ABIDE GLM analysis to account for differences in scan acquisition parameters.

evidence_spans.text:
In the ABIDE GLM analysis, clusters were found that
had greater connectivity with the right thalamus in the
ASD group compared to the TD group. Two of these
clusters were located in the right precentral (p = 0.019)
and postcentral gyri (p = 0.028), validating the observed
hyperconnectivity of the same regions in our HFASD
cohort.
evidence_spans.claim: In the ABIDE validation analysis, right thalamus connectivity with right precentral (p=0.019) and postcentral gyri (p=0.028) was greater in ASD than TD, replicating the primary-cohort finding.

assessments.support: ABIDE subset selection is matched by age, sex and IQ, but the full selection process is deferred to Supplemental Information not present in the extracted full text.
ABIDE demographics (N, age, sex, FSIQ) are tabulated (Table 2) with between-group p-values.
ABIDE data preprocessed identically to the primary cohort with fMRIPrep v1.3.1, with explicit FD-based scrubbing and retention thresholds.
Diagnosis source for the ABIDE subset specifically (vs. the primary HFASD cohort's ADI-R/ADOS confirmation) is not restated in the main text.
Age, sex, IQ matching and motion (FD) are reported and compared between groups; site is explicitly modeled.
Site included as one-hot-encoded covariate in the ABIDE GLM; motion handled via scrubbing and a TR-retention threshold.
Seed-based whole-brain GLM connectivity analysis with the same five a priori seeds as the primary cohort.
Bonferroni correction for five seeds (p=0.01 cluster threshold) is explicitly applied.

risk_of_bias.summary: ABIDE validation cohort is matched and preprocessed identically to the primary cohort with documented motion QC, site covariate handling, and multiple-comparisons correction; main uncertainty is that exact ABIDE inclusion/exclusion selection is deferred to an unretrieved supplement.

charting.title: Towards robust and replicable sex differences in the intrinsic brain function of autism
charting.authors: Dorothea L. Floris; José O. A. Filho; Meng-Chuan Lai; et al.
charting.primary_focus: Sex-by-diagnosis differences in intrinsic brain function
charting.primary_goal: Characterise robust and replicable sex differences and sex-by-diagnosis interactions in resting-state brain function in autism
charting.country_region: Multi-site (13 merged sites from ABIDE I and II)
charting.diagnosis_assessment: ADI-R and ADOS-2 scores available as phenotypic variables (per Table 1 footnotes); confirmation procedure not restated in main text
charting.dataset_openly_available: Yes — ABIDE I and II data freely accessible via the FCP-INDI repository
charting.specific_features: PCC-seed intrinsic functional connectivity (iFC), voxel-mirrored homotopic connectivity (VMHC), regional homogeneity (ReHo), degree centrality (DC), fractional ALFF (fALFF); Harvard-Oxford atlas used for anatomical labelling of clusters
charting.feature_extraction_tools: Custom R-fMRI pipeline (slice-timing correction, 24-parameter motion regression, CompCor, detrending, band-pass filtering, FSL FLIRT BBR + ANTs registration); C-PAC credited in author contributions for analyses support; ComBat (python, brentp/combat.py) for site harmonisation
charting.feature_change_direction: Sex-by-diagnosis interaction: reduced VMHC in autistic females vs. increased/typical VMHC pattern in the other three groups, localized to dorsolateral occipital cortex
charting.validation_methodology: Voxel-level GLM (Z>3.1, cluster-level P<0.01, GRF-corrected); robustness checked across alternative preprocessing pipelines; replication tested in two independent cohorts (EU-AIMS LEAP, GENDAAR)
charting.summary_key_findings: In the ABIDE I+II discovery sample (N=1019, 13 sites), main effects of diagnosis and sex were found across PCC-iFC, ReHo and VMHC converging on the default-network midline; a sex-by-diagnosis interaction on VMHC in dorsolateral occipital cortex showed reduced VMHC in autistic females and replicated in the larger of two independent cohorts (EU-AIMS LEAP) but not GENDAAR.
charting.features_associated_disorder: PCC-iFC, ReHo and VMHC group differences along the default-network midline; VMHC sex-by-diagnosis interaction in dorsolateral occipital cortex
charting.future_directions_recommended: A priori harmonisation across discovery and replication datasets; systematic study of sample-related factors affecting replicability.
charting.reviewer_notes: ABIDE I and II data collections explicitly merged by matched site (e.g., KKI & ABIDEII-KKI1) to form 13 combined sites for ComBat harmonisation.

screening.reason: Inclusion 2-3: ABIDE I+II rs-fMRI functional connectivity used to classify ASD vs TD and to study how population diversity affects predictive accuracy and pattern stability.

evidence_spans.text:
procedures resulted in a total of 297 par-
ticipants (151 ASD and 146 TD) from 4 different sites (i.e., New York University Langone
Medical Center [NYU], University of Pittsburgh, School of Medicine [PITT], University of
Utah, School of Medicine [USM], and Trinity Centre for Health Sciences [TCD]) in ABIDE.
evidence_spans.claim: Final ABIDE sample: 297 participants (151 ASD, 146 TD) from 4 sites (NYU, PITT, USM, TCD).

evidence_spans.text:
For ABIDE, we considered data from all acquisition sites with at least 10 participants per
group and with both children and adults. After detailed quality control, only cases with accept-
able T1-weighted (T1w) MRI, surface extraction, and head motion in rs-fMRI were included.
evidence_spans.claim: ABIDE sites required at least 10 participants per group and both children and adults; QC required acceptable T1w MRI, surface extraction, and acceptable head motion in rs-fMRI.

evidence_spans.text:
Participants with ASD were diagnosed based on an in-person interview administered by
board-certified mental health professionals using the gold standard diagnostics of the Autism
Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) [51] and/or Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised
(ADI-R) [52,53].
evidence_spans.claim: ASD diagnosis was based on an in-person interview using ADOS and/or ADI-R gold-standard diagnostics.

evidence_spans.text:
For the resting-state functional brain scans in ABIDE, we built on data previously made
available by the Preprocessed Connectomes initiative (http://preprocessed-connectomes-
project.org/abide). The preprocessing was performed with C-PAC (https://fcp-indi.github.io)
and included slice time correction, head motion correction, skull stripping, and intensity nor-
malization. The rs-fMRI data were detrended and adjusted for common nuisance effects
related to head motion, white matter, and cerebrospinal fluid signals using CompCor [58], fol-
lowed by band-pass filtering (0.01 to 0.1 Hz).
evidence_spans.claim: ABIDE rs-fMRI was preprocessed via the Preprocessed Connectomes initiative using C-PAC (slice-time correction, motion correction, skull stripping, intensity normalization, CompCor, band-pass filtering).

evidence_spans.text:
Func-
tional connectivity matrices were calculated at a single-participant level based on a widely used
parcellation atlas with 100 cortical regions [61].
evidence_spans.claim: Functional connectivity matrices were computed using a 100-region (Schaefer-Yeo) cortical parcellation atlas.

evidence_spans.text:
After matching, we ended up with 290 participants (145 participants per group)
in ABIDE and 126 (63 participants per group) in HBN, which were used subsequently for the
classification of ASD versus TD in both datasets.
evidence_spans.claim: After propensity-score matching on age, sex and site, 290 ABIDE participants (145 per group) were used for classification.

evidence_spans.text:
Similar to the computation of the pro-
pensity scores, we performed deconfounding prior to our analyses, based on all the available
participants instead of using only the training
evidence_spans.claim: Propensity scores and deconfounding were computed using all available participants rather than training data only.

evidence_spans.text:
In the ABIDE cohort, when we trained and
tested on data with similar distributions (first column), the contiguous scheme reached better
prediction performance than the diverse scheme, with the random scheme lying in between.
This trend remained stable as we increased the number of strata used for training.
evidence_spans.claim: In ABIDE, training and testing on similarly-distributed (contiguous) strata achieved better prediction than diverse strata.

evidence_spans.text:
we can observe a decline in performance in ABIDE as diversity increased in both within
(AUC: r = −0.630, F1 score: r = −0.568) and out-of-distribution (AUC: r = −0.671, F1 score:

charting.title: Population heterogeneity in clinical cohorts affects the predictive accuracy of brain imaging
charting.authors: Oualid Benkarim; Casey Paquola; Bo-yong Park; et al.
charting.primary_focus: Effect of population heterogeneity/diversity on predictive accuracy and pattern stability
charting.primary_goal: Quantify how demographic/site diversity (via propensity scores) affects cross-validated prediction accuracy and biomarker pattern stability in ASD classification
charting.country_region: Multi-site (4 ABIDE sites: NYU, PITT, USM, TCD)
charting.diagnosis_assessment: ADOS and/or ADI-R gold-standard diagnostics via in-person interview by board-certified mental health professionals
charting.n_disordered: 151 (297 total before matching); 145 after propensity-score matching
charting.comorbidities_included_excluded: Excluded: genetic disorders associated with autism (e.g. Fragile X), MRI contraindications, current pregnancy
charting.n_controls: 146 (297 total before matching); 145 after propensity-score matching
charting.age_matched: true (propensity-score matched on age, sex, site)
charting.dataset_openly_available: Yes — all imaging features, phenotypic data and analysis code openly available at https://github.com/OualidBenkarim/ps_diversity; figure data in S1 Data
charting.specific_features: Region-to-region functional connectivity using a 100-region Schaefer-Yeo cortical parcellation atlas
charting.feature_extraction_tools: C-PAC (Preprocessed Connectomes Project pipeline: slice-time correction, motion correction, skull stripping, intensity normalization, CompCor, band-pass filtering 0.01-0.1 Hz); FreeSurfer for structural/cortical thickness
charting.importance_method: Model coefficient (weight vector) consistency via Pearson correlation across resampled models
charting.model_category: Linear classifier (predictive modeling of ASD vs TD from functional connectivity)
charting.validation_methodology: Propensity-score-based stratified train/holdout partitioning (contiguous, diverse, random sampling schemes) with 10-fold CV within training strata; out-of-distribution evaluation on held-out strata
charting.key_performance_results: ABIDE: prediction performance declined as diversity increased — within-distribution AUC r=-0.630, F1 r=-0.568; out-of-distribution AUC r=-0.671, F1 r=-0.579. Deconfounding (linear regression r=-0.539; ComBat r=-0.599) only slightly reduced this correlation versus raw data (r=-0.671).
charting.summary_key_findings: In ABIDE (and oppositely in HBN), predictive accuracy and pattern stability for ASD vs TD classification decline substantially as population diversity (quantified via propensity scores on age, sex, site) increases, and this effect persists after standard deconfounding (linear regression or ComBat), which were themselves computed using all participants rather than training data only.
charting.reviewer_notes: Important methodological finding: propensity-score and deconfounding computations used the full dataset (not train-only), a leakage concern the authors themselves report.

narrative_row.relevance_notes: Directly interrogates how ABIDE's site/demographic composition (diversity) affects reproducibility of predictive findings; open code and data make the analysed cohort reconstructible; illustrates a leakage pattern (full-sample deconfounding) relevant to RQ4/CL5 across the corpus.

evidence_spans.claim: The released ABIDE I dataset of 1,112 samples was reduced to 1,035 after preprocessing and quality control.
MADE-for-ASD achieved 75.20% accuracy (82.90% sensitivity, 69.70% specificity) on the whole dataset (N=1035), 88.71% on a proposed subset (N=645), and 96.40% on the NYU subset (N=175).

evidence_spans.text:
The Automated Anatomical Labelling (AAL) atlas, with 116 ROIs, is widely
used in ASD diagnosis studies [16, 35, 36, 37] due to its ability to provide precise anatomical lo-
cations essential for identifying structural abnormalities caused by ASD. The Craddock 200 atlas
[38], with 200 ROIs, is based on functional connectivity and is particularly useful for analysing
resting-state fMRI data [39, 9, 36, 37], as it clusters the brain into functionally homogeneous
regions.
Recent studies have leveraged multiple atlases to capture diverse patterns related to ASD.
For instance, Mahler et al. [37] proposed a multi-atlas framework for ASD classification using
resting-state fMRI data, employing three atlases, including AAL and Craddock 200. Similarly,
Deng et al. [9] utilised the AAL, Craddock 200 and Craddock 400 atlases. Their experiment in-
dicates that Craddock 200 can outperform Craddock 400 in fMRI-based ASD diagnosis. Hence,
we selected the Craddock 200 atlas, hereinafter referred to as the CC atlas.
To further enhance the analysis, we leverage the Eickhoff-Zilles (EZ) atlas with 116 ROIs,
which has also been utilised in recent ASD diagnosis studies [40, 41]. Derived from cytoarchi-
tectonic mapping, the EZ atlas combines anatomical and functional data, offering a nuanced view
that bridges structural and functional aspects of brain regions
evidence_spans.claim: Three atlases were used: AAL (116 ROIs), Craddock 200 (CC), and Eickhoff-Zilles (EZ).

evidence_spans.text:
Our model achieved an ac-
curacy score of 75.20%, which is a boost of 4.4 percentage points over the best prior work [20]
on 1,035 samples.
evidence_spans.claim: The model improved accuracy by 4.4 percentage points over the best prior work on the same 1,035-sample ABIDE I CPAC dataset.

assessments.support: Raw (1,112) and post-QC (1,035: 505 ASD, 530 TC) Ns, plus NYU subset (182->175) and demographic feature availability, are explicitly reported.
CPAC pipeline (one of four Preprocessed Connectomes Project pipelines) and three named atlases (AAL, CC200, EZ) are explicitly reported.
ASD vs TC labels are taken directly from the ABIDE I release; the diagnostic-instrument source is not independently restated in the main text.

Two leakage-relevant practices: (1) F-score feature selection is described as computed 'for all features in the dataset' rather than confined to training folds; (2) the 'proposed subset' (N=645, accuracy 88.71%) is defined by a pretrained selector model's own correct classifications on the whole dataset, so performance on that subset is tautologically inflated by construction rather than reflecting genuine held-out generalisation.

risk_of_bias.summary: Transparent, code-released, multi-atlas predictive study on ABIDE I with reported 10-fold CV and SOTA whole-dataset accuracy (75.20%), but the 'proposed subset' evaluation (88.71% accuracy) is constructed by selecting samples the classifier itself got right, and F-score feature selection is described as using the whole dataset rather than training folds only — both raise PROBAST Analysis-domain leakage concerns.

charting.title: MADE-for-ASD: A multi-atlas deep ensemble network for diagnosing Autism Spectrum Disorder
charting.authors: Xuehan Liu; Md Rakibul Hasan; et al.
charting.primary_goal: Diagnose ASD vs typical controls from ABIDE I rs-fMRI functional connectivity plus demographic data using a weighted deep ensemble network
charting.data_types: resting-state fMRI, demographic data (age, sex, handedness, FIQ)
charting.dataset_openly_available: Code and evaluations publicly available at https://github.com/hasan-rakibul/MADE-for-ASD
charting.specific_features: Functional connectivity matrices from AAL (116 ROIs), Craddock 200 (CC), and Eickhoff-Zilles (EZ) atlases; top features selected via F-score
charting.feature_extraction_tools: CPAC pipeline (Preprocessed Connectomes Project)
charting.importance_method: F-score ranking

charting.model_category: Deep ensemble (stacked sparse denoising autoencoder + MLP, weighted voting)
charting.specific_algorithms: SSDAE+MLP ensemble (MADE-for-ASD)
charting.validation_methodology: 10-fold cross-validation; evaluated on whole ABIDE I CPAC dataset, a data-selector-defined 'proposed subset', and the NYU site subset
charting.key_performance_results: Whole dataset (N=1035): 75.20% accuracy, 82.90% sensitivity, 69.70% specificity. Proposed subset (N=645): 88.71% accuracy. NYU subset (N=175): 96.40% accuracy, 91.00% sensitivity, 99.50% specificity.
charting.summary_key_findings: MADE-for-ASD achieves 75.20% accuracy on the whole ABIDE I CPAC dataset (N=1035), a 4.4-percentage-point improvement over prior SOTA on the same data, with higher accuracy (88.71%, 96.40%) on a self-selected 'proposed subset' and the NYU site subset respectively; demographic information and multi-atlas fusion are reported to improve performance.
charting.future_directions_recommended: Improve interpretation of fMRI-derived features relative to autism symptoms; extend interpretability and clinical correlation of deep learning outputs.
charting.reviewer_notes: The 'proposed subset' (645/1035, 88.71% accuracy) is defined as samples a pretrained selector model itself classified correctly — this is a circularity/leakage concern when reporting that subset's accuracy as a performance result.

charting.title: Promises, Pitfalls, and Basic Guidelines for Applying Machine Learning Classifiers to Psychiatric Imaging Data, with Autism as an Example
charting.primary_focus: Diagnosis / methodological tutorial on ML classification pitfalls
charting.primary_goal: Demonstrate and compare ML classification pipelines for ASD vs TD using ABIDE RS-fMRI data, while teaching methodological pitfalls (peeking/double-dipping, site effects)
charting.dataset_openly_available: MATLAB code for all pipelines publicly available (ETH website)
charting.specific_features: 200x200 Craddock-atlas ROI-to-ROI Pearson correlation matrix (19,900 features)
charting.feature_extraction_tools: SPM12 (realignment, DARTEL normalization, smoothing, band-pass filter 0.01-0.05Hz, motion scrubbing)
charting.importance_method: Mean-difference threshold feature selection (t-value threshold), with nested CV for threshold tuning
charting.model_category: Multiple classical ML classifiers compared
charting.specific_algorithms: Logistic regression, lasso-regularized logistic regression, linear SVM, probabilistic neural network, linear discriminant analysis, Gaussian naive Bayes
charting.validation_methodology: Nested 10x10-fold cross-validation (outer loop for performance, inner loop for feature-selection/tuning-parameter selection); explicit avoidance of double-dipping via train-only feature selection and standardization
charting.key_performance_results: LR 58%, LassoLR 58%, SVM 63% (best out-of-the-box), PNN 58%, LDA 57%, GNB 61% accuracy; SVM accuracy increased to 68% after per-site (train-only) z-standardization; all classifiers significantly better than chance (p<0.001).
charting.summary_key_findings: Out-of-the-box ML classifiers applied correctly (nested CV) to ABIDE rs-fMRI connectivity achieve about 60-70% accuracy (best: SVM 63%, improving to 68% with site standardization); incorrect feature selection on the full dataset ('peeking'/double-dipping) can spuriously inflate accuracy to 91% in a null simulation, illustrating a major pitfall in the field.
charting.future_directions_recommended: Leave-one-site-out cross-validation and further site-effect correction beyond linear z-transformation; stable feature selection methods for biomarker interpretation.
charting.reviewer_notes: A methods/tutorial paper that nonetheless performs an original classification analysis on real ABIDE data; valuable as a positive worked example of leakage-avoidance practice for the review's CL5 checklist item.

assessments.support: Raw N (1112) and post-QC N (1111: 573 controls, 538 ASD) by diagnosis are reported, with training/test split sizes given.
A custom SPM8-based preprocessing pipeline with HOG voxel-based features is described, but no atlas/parcellation is used since features are image-texture based rather than ROI connectivity.

Feature selection (MRMR) and hyperparameter tuning were performed via 5-fold cross-validation strictly on the training set, with final evaluation on a completely held-out test set never used during model/feature selection — an explicit leakage-avoidance design. risk_of_bias.summary: Methodologically careful train/hold-out split with feature selection and tuning confined to the training set (avoiding peeking), but site is included as a raw predictive feature rather than harmonised, and no connectivity atlas/parcellation or explicit motion-metric threshold is reported.

charting.title: Using Functional or Structural Magnetic Resonance Images and Personal Characteristic Data to Identify ADHD and Autism
charting.primary_goal: Build a single automated learning pipeline (MHPC) to classify ADHD (ADHD-200) and autism (ABIDE) from functional/structural MRI and personal characteristic data
charting.country_region: Multi-site (17 institutions, North America and Europe)
charting.data_types: resting-state fMRI, structural MRI, personal characteristic data (age, sex, handedness, IQ measures, site, eye status)
charting.dataset_openly_available: Yes — ABIDE and ADHD-200 datasets are both publicly available online; no separate analysis code repository mentioned
charting.feature_types: Voxel-based image texture (3D Histogram of Oriented Gradients) + personal characteristic data
charting.specific_features: 3D-HOG features extracted from functional or structural MRI (no ROI/atlas parcellation); feature selection via minimum-redundancy-maximum-relevance (MRMR)
charting.feature_extraction_tools: SPM8 + in-house MATLAB preprocessing pipeline (motion correction, co-registration, spatial normalization to MNI)
charting.importance_method: MRMR feature selection; features mapped back to brain regions
charting.model_category: Ensemble of classical ML base learners (MHPC system)
charting.specific_algorithms: Linear SVM, RBF-kernel SVM, decision trees, k-nearest neighbours, naive Bayes
charting.validation_methodology: 5-fold cross-validation on the training set for feature selection (MRMR) and hyperparameter tuning; final single evaluation on a held-out test set (889 train / 222 test, label-balanced random split)
charting.key_performance_results: ABIDE hold-out: Functional MRI 59.2% (baseline 51.6%), Structural MRI 60.1%, Personal Characteristic 59.6%, Structural+PCD 64.1%, Functional+PCD 65.0% (best) accuracy.
charting.summary_key_findings: Combining resting-state fMRI-derived HOG features with personal characteristic data achieved the best ABIDE hold-out accuracy of 65.0% (baseline 51.6%), outperforming functional MRI alone (59.2%), structural MRI alone (60.1%), and PCD alone (59.6%), and outperforming the then-best published ABIDE result (60.0% over a 53.6% baseline).
charting.reviewer_notes: Site of imaging is used as an input feature rather than harmonised away or held out, which may let the classifier partly learn site identity rather than purely disorder-related signal.

evidence_spans.text:
We used resting state fMRI data of 458 subjects with ASD and
517 TDCs (see Table 1 for additional demographic information)
among 1112 datasets from the ABIDE datasets
evidence_spans.claim: 458 ASD and 517 TDC subjects were selected from 1112 ABIDE datasets.

evidence_spans.text:
We excluded
datasets from the social brain Lab BCN NIC UMC Groningen
and Netherlands Institute for Neurosciences due to the missing
information of a full-scale intelligence quotient (IQ) for many
subjects. After preprocessing, we found that a large part of the
cerebellum was missing in the imaging dataset of Carnegie
Mellon University, and all datasets from Carnegie Mellon
University were excluded. To control for potential confounding
eﬀects of IQ in our analysis, we decided to exclude ﬁve datasets
that included some subjects with IQ lower than 70. Finally, we
performed voxel-wise group comparisons with 975 imaging
datasets.
evidence_spans.claim: Sites/datasets were excluded for missing FIQ (Groningen), incomplete cerebellar coverage (Carnegie Mellon), or low IQ (<70, five further datasets), leaving 975 datasets for voxel-wise comparison.

evidence_spans.text:
Datasets were preprocessed with SPM8 (http://www.ﬁl.ion.ucl.
ac.uk/spm/software/spm8/). The ﬁrst step was realignment for
head motion correction. Images were realigned to the ﬁrst
image and a mean echo planar image (EPI) was created during
this step. Subsequently, structural T1 images were coregistered
to their mean EPI data. Registered EPI data of each subject
were normalized to Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI)
template and spatially smoothed with 8 mm of full-width at half-
maximum. Then, in the temporal domain, the linearly increasing
trend due to heat absorption was removed at each voxel, and
the eﬀects of the head motion, white matter, cerebrospinal ﬂuid,
and global signal were regressed out. Lastly, temporal band-pass
ﬁltering was applied (0.01–0.08 Hz).
evidence_spans.claim: Data were preprocessed with SPM8: realignment, coregistration, MNI normalization, 8mm smoothing, detrending, nuisance regression (motion, WM, CSF, global signal), band-pass filtering.

evidence_spans.text:
2-tailed t-test design with two covariates of age
and sex was used to compute the statistical signiﬁcance of the
FCD diﬀerences between the two groups. Statistical signiﬁcance
was based on the false discovery rate corrected P < 0.05 together
with requiring 20 voxels for the minimum continuous voxel
size within a cluster (corrected P < 0.05).
evidence_spans.claim: Group differences were tested with a 2-tailed t-test (age and sex covariates), FDR-corrected P<0.05 with a minimum cluster size of 20 voxels.

evidence_spans.claim: Clinical diagnosis-related measures used included ADI-R, ADOS-RRB, and ADOS-COM subscores from the ABIDE phenotypic data.

assessments.support: Explicit site/IQ/coverage-based exclusion rules and resulting N (975 of 1112) are reported.
458 ASD and 517 TDC from a defined subset of ABIDE sites, with demographics in Table 1.
SPM8 preprocessing pipeline with standard nuisance regression and band-pass filtering is explicitly described.
ADI-R and ADOS (RRB, COM) clinical measures from the ABIDE phenotypic data are used and correlated with connectivity.

Age and sex are modeled as covariates; head motion is regressed as a nuisance signal, but no explicit motion-based subject-exclusion threshold (e.g. FD cutoff) is reported; site is not included as a covariate despite pooling 15 sites.
Age/sex covariates and motion nuisance regression are used, but no site covariate or harmonisation is applied despite acknowledged multi-site heterogeneity.
Voxel-wise global/inter-/intra-hemispheric functional connectivity density (FCD) is a clearly defined, previously validated data-driven metric.
FDR correction (P<0.05) with a minimum cluster size of 20 voxels, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction for correlation analyses.

risk_of_bias.summary: Cohort definition, preprocessing and multiple-comparisons correction are transparently reported, but no motion-based subject-exclusion threshold or site covariate/harmonisation is described despite pooling 15 ABIDE sites, leaving residual site-confound risk in the Analysis/Confounders domains.

evidence_spans.text: Our results show that the proposed model achieves state of the art results on single sites with F1-scores of 0.78 and 0.7 on NYU and UM sites, respectively.

evidence_spans.text: For single sites experiments, we use the NYU and UM sites from ABIDE-I. Those provide the highest number of balanced (ASD/typically developing (TD)) subjects with 184 and 110 subjects respectively.
evidence_spans.claim: Single-site cohorts: NYU 184 subjects, UM 110 subjects.

evidence_spans.text: For the multi-site experiment we used ABIDE-I with 19 sites and 1100 subjects.
evidence_spans.claim: Multi-site cohort: 19 ABIDE-I sites, 1100 subjects.

evidence_spans.text: We report 5-fold cross validation mean F1-score and accuracy for the experiments in Table 1.
evidence_spans.claim: Evaluation uses 5-fold cross-validation (no leave-site-out scheme described).

evidence_spans.text: The results show that the proposed architecture 3DCNN C-LSTM outperforms other models on single site experiments by achieving mean test accuracies and F1 scores of 0.77 and 0.78 respectively for the NYU site and 0.71 and 0.7 on the UM site.

evidence_spans.text:
3DCNN C-LSTM however also shows a degraded performance in multi-site
environment as evidenced by the results on ABIDE-1 data that features 19 sites.
evidence_spans.claim: Performance degrades on the multi-site ABIDE-I evaluation relative to single-site.

evidence_spans.text:
We attribute the loss of performance of our model to the heterogeneity of the
data acquired from diﬀerent scanners with diﬀerent scanning parameters.
evidence_spans.claim: Authors attribute multi-site performance loss to scanner/acquisition heterogeneity.

evidence_spans.text: The proposed MGRL is evaluated on 184 subjects from the public Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) database with rs-fMRI scans.
evidence_spans.claim: Primary evaluation cohort: 184 ABIDE subjects.

evidence_spans.text: In this work, we use rs-fMRI data from the New York University (NYU) site with the largest sample size collected in this database. Speciﬁcally, the NYU site includes 184 subjects, 79 of whom were from ASD and 105 NC cases.
evidence_spans.claim: Primary cohort: NYU site, 79 ASD, 105 NC.

evidence_spans.text: the remaining volumes are processed by a well- accepted pipeline with the Data Processing Assistant for Resting- State fMRI toolbox (DPARSF) (Yan et al., 2016).
evidence_spans.claim: Preprocessing pipeline: DPARSF.

evidence_spans.text: by partitioning the brain into multiple ROIs using two atlases, i.e., Automated Anatomical Labeling (AAL) (Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2002) atlas with 116 ROIs and Craddock200 (CC200) (Craddock et al., 2012) atlas with 200 ROIs.
evidence_spans.claim: Multi-scale atlases: AAL (116 ROIs) and CC200 (200 ROIs).

evidence_spans.text:
Considering the small amount of subjects, we randomly select
80% of all the samples as training data, 10% of all samples as
validation data, and the remaining 10% as test data. We repeat the
random partition process 100 times and record the mean and SD
results of each method.
evidence_spans.claim: Validation: random 80/10/10 train/val/test split repeated 100 times, mean±SD reported.
MGRL main NYU result: accuracy 0.795, recall 0.809, precision 0.823, F1 0.802, AUC 0.886.

evidence_spans.text: to avoid signiﬁcant inter-site heterogeneity, we mainly used rs-fMRI data from the NYU site. While ABIDE contains data from 21 sites, as a future work, we will evaluate the proposed method on all sites in ABIDE and design smart techniques to reduce inter-site data heterogeneity.
evidence_spans.claim: Authors deliberately restricted to single sites (NYU/UM) to avoid inter-site heterogeneity; no multi-site/leave-site-out evaluation performed.

screening.reason: Inclusion 2,3: resting-state fMRI group-difference analysis (ASD vs HC) on ABIDE I, used as one of two multi-site test cases for a site-effect mitigation method (site-wise de-meaning), with an ASD-vs-control effect-size evaluation (not a software-only benchmark, since it quantifies preservation of a known autism-vs-control FC finding).

evidence_spans.text: We present a site-wise de-meaning (SWD) strategy in multi-site FC analysis and compare its performance with two common site-effect mitigation methods, i.e., generalized linear model (GLM) and Combining Batches (ComBat) Harmonization.
evidence_spans.claim: Main method: site-wise de-meaning (SWD) compared against GLM and ComBat for multi-site FC harmonisation.

evidence_spans.text: Resting-state fMRI data from 850 subjects in ABIDE I with an ASD DSM-IV-TR diagnosis (n = 355) and the corresponding HCs (n = 495) from the same sites were used in this study
evidence_spans.claim: Analysed ABIDE I cohort: 355 ASD, 495 HC (850 total).

Age and sex are regressed out ("linear regression was used to regress out age
and sex covariates"); site is the central confounder the entire paper is designed to address.
Site effects handled via three compared methods (GLM, ComBat, and the proposed site-wise de-meaning), directly testing which best preserves the diagnostic group effect.
Pearson correlation FC, Fisher z-transformed, with Hedge's g effect size relative to a literature-anchored finding (anterior-posterior DMN hypoconnectivity).

Effect sizes (Hedge's g) are reported for specific literature-selected ROI pairs rather than a whole-brain corrected statistical test, so multiple-comparison correction is not directly applicable/reported for this effect-size preservation analysis.

screening.reason: Reports a diagnostic prediction (3D CNN autism vs. control classification) analysis of ABIDE I and ABIDE II resting-state fMRI connectivity (Inclusion 2, 3; not excluded by 1-6).

evidence_spans.text: We showcase our approach on a challenging large-scale dataset (ABIDE, with N > 2, 000) and report state-of-the-art accuracy results on rs-fMRI- based discrimination of autism patients and healthy controls.
evidence_spans.claim: The study classifies autism vs. control using ABIDE resting-state fMRI connectomes with a 3D CNN.

evidence_spans.text: The ﬁrst phase of ABIDE (ABIDE-I) compiled data from 1112 individuals, comprising 539 individuals diagnosed with Autism Spec- trum Disorder (ASD) and 573 typical controls, from 17 sites. The second phase (ABIDE-II) was recently released, and consists of an additional 521 individuals with ASD and 593 healthy controls, from 19 sites.
evidence_spans.claim: Describes the full ABIDE I and ABIDE II releases used as the data source.

evidence_spans.text: In our experiments, we used ABIDE-I subject data that passed manual qual- ity assessments (QA) by all the functional raters. This yielded a ﬁnal sample size of 774 ABIDE-I subjects, comprising 379 subjects with ASD and 395 typical con- trols.
evidence_spans.claim: ABIDE-I analysed subset: 774 subjects (379 ASD, 395 TD) selected by manual QA.

evidence_spans.text: Since manual QA was not yet available for ABIDE-II, we per- formed an automatic quality control by selecting those subjects that retained at least 100 frames or 4 minutes of fMRI scans after motion scrubbing [19]. Motion scrubbing was performed based on Framewise Displacement (FD), dis- carding one volume before and two volumes after the frame with FD exceeding 0.5mm [15]. This step yielded a ﬁnal ABIDE-II sample size of 163 individuals with ASD and 230 healthy controls.
evidence_spans.claim: ABIDE-II held-out test subset (163 ASD, 230 TD) defined by an automatic motion-scrubbing QC rule (FD > 0.5mm, minimum 100 retained frames).

evidence_spans.text: The Preprocessed Connectomes Project (PCP) released preprocessed versions of ABIDE using several pipelines [4]. We used the data processed through Conﬁgurable Pipeline for Analysis of Connectomes (CPAC). This pipeline includes slice timing correction, motion correction, global mean intensity normalization and standardization of functional data to MNI space (3x3x3 mm resolution) before the extraction of ROI time series.
evidence_spans.claim: Preprocessing used the PCP CPAC pipeline.

evidence_spans.text: First, we implemented a 10-fold cross-validation scheme for ABIDE-I to be consistent with previously reported classiﬁcation re- sults [1, 18]. Second, we trained each model on all of ABIDE-I and computed test performance on an independent held-out set from ABIDE-II. This is used for assessing the generalization behavior of diﬀerent classiﬁers. We report accu- racy and the receiver operating curves (ROC), along with corresponding area under the curves (AUC) for each of these scenarios.
evidence_spans.claim: Evaluation used 10-fold CV on ABIDE-I plus an independent held-out test on ABIDE-II, reporting accuracy and AUC.

evidence_spans.text: Previous studies have reported cross- validated classiﬁcation accuracies up to 67% on ABIDE-I, the ﬁrst phase of the ABIDE study [1]. The proposed CNN approach improves this accuracy to above 73%.
evidence_spans.claim: The proposed 3D-CNN improves cross-validated ABIDE-I accuracy from a prior benchmark of 67% to above 73%.

evidence_spans.text: The ensemble achieves an AUC of 75.8%.
evidence_spans.claim: The atlas-ensemble CNN achieves an AUC of 75.8% on the ABIDE-II independent test.

assessments.support: Cohort composition and QC-based exclusion are explicitly reported for both ABIDE-I (manual QA, n=774) and ABIDE-II (automatic motion-scrubbing QC, n=393): "In our experiments, we used ABIDE-I subject data that passed manual qual- ity assessments (QA) by all the functional raters. This yielded a ﬁnal sample size of 774 ABIDE-I subjects, comprising 379 subjects with ASD and 395 typical con- trols."
Pipeline (CPAC/PCP, version noted for ABIDE-II) and seven atlases (HO, EZ, TT, CC200, CC400, AAL, DOS160) are named with preprocessing steps described.
Diagnostic label source (how ASD/TD status was determined in ABIDE) is not described in this paper beyond citing the ABIDE release.

Design uses 10-fold CV plus a fully independent ABIDE-II test set (reduces leakage for the main CNN), but baseline hyperparameters were selected by maximising cross-validation accuracy itself, which the authors acknowledge is optimistic: "We test 10 linearly spaced values for the hyper-parameter α in the range [0.1,10] and report the highest cross-validation accuracy. Thus this baseline result reﬂects an optimistic estimate of performance."; no explicit site covariate/harmonisation, and ABIDE-II test sites overlap with ABIDE-I training sites.

risk_of_bias.summary: Cohort and preprocessing are clearly reported; outcome/label source is not described, and the baseline models' hyperparameter selection is self-acknowledged as leakage-optimistic, while the primary CNN is evaluated on an independent ABIDE-II hold-out but without site covariate handling.

narrative_row.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction (3D CNN) using ABIDE-I (10-fold CV training set, n=774: 379 ASD/395 TD, 17 sites) and ABIDE-II (independent held-out test, n=393: 163 ASD/230 TD, sites overlapping ABIDE-I).
narrative_row.methods: CPAC/PCP-preprocessed connectivity fingerprints across seven atlases fed into a volumetric 3D CNN; compared against ridge regression, linear SVM, and fully-connected DNN baselines; evaluated via 10-fold CV on ABIDE-I and an independent held-out test on ABIDE-II.
narrative_row.outcomes: 3D-CNN atlas-ensemble reached 73.3% CV accuracy (ABIDE-I) and 71.7% independent test accuracy (ABIDE-II), AUC 75.8% on the ABIDE-II test, outperforming all baselines and a prior ABIDE-I benchmark of up to 67%.
narrative_row.key_limitations: No code/participant-list availability statement; baseline hyperparameters tuned by maximising CV accuracy (acknowledged optimistic); no explicit site covariate/harmonisation; ABIDE-II test sites overlap with ABIDE-I training sites rather than being fully held out; diagnostic label source not described.
narrative_row.relevance_notes: Demonstrates volumetric 3D-CNN classification with atlas-ensemble voting, trained on ABIDE-I and externally validated on an independent ABIDE-II cohort; a cross-release external-validation example linking the two ABIDE phases.

evidence_quotes: In our experiments, we used ABIDE-I subject data that passed manual qual- ity assessments (QA) by all the functional raters. This yielded a ﬁnal sample size of 774 ABIDE-I subjects, comprising 379 subjects with ASD and 395 typical con- trols.

Since manual QA was not yet available for ABIDE-II, we per- formed an automatic quality control by selecting those subjects that retained at least 100 frames or 4 minutes of fMRI scans after motion scrubbing [19]. Motion scrubbing was performed based on Framewise Displacement (FD), dis- carding one volume before and two volumes after the frame with FD exceeding 0.5mm [15]. This step yielded a ﬁnal ABIDE-II sample size of 163 individuals with ASD and 230 healthy controls.

screening.reason: Trains ML models on the IMPAC dataset and reports a resting-state-fMRI-based external validation (AUROC) of those models on ABIDE I and ABIDE II (Inclusion 2, 3; ABIDE used for an autism-vs-control predictive analysis, not merely cited).

evidence_spans.text: Our model achieves state-of-the-art 80% area under the ROC curve (AUROC) in diagnosis on test data from the IMPAC dataset; and 86% and 79% AUROC on the external ABIDE I and ABIDE II datasets (with further improvement to 93% and 90% after supervised domain adaptation).
evidence_spans.claim: Models trained on IMPAC generalise to ABIDE I and ABIDE II with 86% and 79% AUROC, improving to 93%/90% after supervised domain adaptation.

evidence_spans.text: Participants from all sites of the ABIDE I and ABIDE II were included for external validation, provided both sMRI and rsfMRI were obtained on the same visit. The first avail- able pair of sMRI and rsfMRI scans were used per subject. 1045 subjects from ABIDE I and 761 subjects from ABIDE II met this criteria.
evidence_spans.claim: External validation used all ABIDE I/II sites, restricted to subjects with a paired same-visit sMRI+rsfMRI scan: 1045 ABIDE I and 761 ABIDE II subjects.

evidence_spans.text: The IMPAC fMRI and sMRI were processed using the fconn1000 ­pipeline41. For the fMRI connectivity features, the TSE connectivity metric was fit on either the training data alone (IMPAC models) or the entire IMPAC dataset (ABIDE 1 and 2 datasets), and the TSE values per-ROI timeseries for the ABIDE dataset were calculated.
evidence_spans.claim: Processing pipeline (fconn1000) and feature-embedding (TSE) procedure for IMPAC and ABIDE connectivity features.

evidence_spans.text: The features were standard scaled by the mean and standard deviation of the IMPAC dataset.
evidence_spans.claim: ABIDE features were scaled using the IMPAC (training) dataset's mean/SD, not refit on ABIDE itself, limiting cross-dataset leakage.

evidence_spans.text: The top single model trained using IMPAC attained 80.4% AUROC on IMPAC held-out test data. When tested on ABIDE I, it achieved an AUROC of 86.0% (Table 2 underlined) and when tested on the ABIDE II it achieved a performance of 79.2%.
evidence_spans.claim: The top IMPAC-trained model achieved 86.0% AUROC on ABIDE I and 79.2% AUROC on ABIDE II without adaptation.

evidence_spans.text: These tuned models achieved AUROC as high as 93.2% on ABIDE-I and 90.5% on ABIDE-II, roughly a 4–9 basis point increase in performance relative to models without any adaptation.
evidence_spans.claim: Supervised domain adaptation raised AUROC to 93.2% on ABIDE-I and 90.5% on ABIDE-II.

narrative_row.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction (federated learning) using ABIDE I resting-state fMRI from four sites: NYU (n=167: 73 ASD/94 HC), UM1 (n=88: 43/45), USM (n=52: 33/19), UCLA1 (n=63: 37/26).
narrative_row.methods: CPAC-preprocessed ROI time series (Harvard-Oxford atlas, 0.01-0.1Hz band-pass, no GSR; CC200 atlas as replication) fed into MLP classifiers trained under a privacy-preserving federated-learning framework, with two domain-adaptation extensions (MoE, adversarial alignment); compared against single-site, cross-site, ensemble and pooled (Mix) training via 5-fold CV.
narrative_row.outcomes: Federated learning (Fed) outperformed single-site and best cross-site training at every site (accuracy 0.647-0.849 across sites, HO atlas) and approached pooled (Mix) accuracy without centralising data; domain adaptation further improved accuracy at most sites; results replicated (at lower absolute accuracy) with the CC200 atlas.
narrative_row.key_limitations: No motion/FD-based QC rule or statistical site harmonisation (e.g. ComBat) reported; diagnostic label source not described; no code/participant-list availability statement; class balance (ASD%) varies by site (44-63%) without an explicit correction.
narrative_row.relevance_notes: Demonstrates that privacy-preserving federated learning across four ABIDE I sites can approach the accuracy of pooled multi-site training without data sharing, directly relevant to the dataset's distributed, multi-site structure.

screening.reason: Reports a diagnostic prediction (ASD vs. control) analysis using resting-state fMRI (plus structural MRI) functional connectivity/ICA features from ABIDE, alongside an ADHD-200 analysis (Inclusion 2, 3).

evidence_spans.text: achieving an accuracy of 0.673 on the ADHD-200 holdout data and 0.643 on the ABIDE holdout data. Both of these results, obtained with the same LEFMSF framework, are the best known, over all hold-out accuracies on these datasets when only using imaging data—exceeding previously-published results by 0.012 for ADHD and 0.042 for Autism.
evidence_spans.claim: The combined structural+functional learner (LEFMSF) achieves 0.643 hold-out accuracy on ABIDE, the best known result using imaging data alone at the time, exceeding prior work by 0.042.

evidence_spans.text: The ABIDE dataset consists of 1111 scans, taken from 17 sites consisting of 573 healthy controls and 538 patients with autism. To evaluate each learning model, we use 800 subjects (70%) for model training and 311 subjects (30%) for hold-out testing. We use the same case/control ratio (0.5157) for both training and test set.
evidence_spans.claim: ABIDE: 1111 scans from 17 sites (573 HC, 538 ASD), split 800 (70%) training / 311 (30%) hold-out test, preserving the case:control ratio in both sets.

evidence_spans.text: For preprocessing fMRI and MRI scans, we used SPM8 (http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/ software/spm8/) and our own in-house MATLAB code. Preprocessing was identical to that used in Ghiassian et al. [13].
evidence_spans.claim: Preprocessing used SPM8 plus in-house MATLAB code, identical to a prior published pipeline (Ghiassian et al.).

evidence_spans.text: the resulting hold-out accuracy for ADHD was 0.6491 (baseline 0.5497) and was 0.6233 for ABIDE (baseline 0.5157). The specificity, sensitivity and Jstat for ADHD (resp., ABIDE) are 0.8191, 0.4416 and 0.2607 (respectively, 0.6768, 0.5533 and 0.2301). To our knowl- edge, our holdout accuracies achieved on ADHD-200 test data and the ABIDE test data are the best known when only using fMRI scans.
evidence_spans.claim: Hold-out accuracy was 0.6233 for ABIDE (baseline 0.5157), described as the best known result using fMRI scans alone.

evidence_spans.text: We found that models trained using only site information achieved an accuracy of 66.0% on the ADHD data and 55.0% on the ABIDE data, while our models trained on MRI data achieved much higher accuracies: 67.4% and 64.3%, respectively.
evidence_spans.claim: A model using only site identity achieved just 55.0% accuracy on ABIDE, far below the 64.3% achieved using MRI-derived features, indicating the classifier is not simply exploiting site identity.

evidence_spans.text: We then tested those previously-trained classifiers on these new “site-balanced test sets” and found that the accuracies did not differ significantly from the original test set results: here, it was 69.88% for ADHD-200 and 63.46% for ABIDE.
evidence_spans.claim: Accuracy on site-balanced (50:50 case:control per site) test sets was 63.46% for ABIDE, not significantly different from the original test set, confirming the result is not a site-composition artifact.

evidence_spans.text: Both datasets are available online publicly. The ADHD-200 dataset is available at: http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/ indi/adhd200/ The ABIDE dataset is available at: (http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/abide/).
evidence_spans.claim: Both the ADHD-200 and ABIDE datasets used are publicly available online.

assessments.support: ABIDE cohort composition, sites, and the train/hold-out split (preserving case:control ratio) are explicit: "The ABIDE dataset consists of 1111 scans, taken from 17 sites consisting of 573 healthy controls and 538 patients with autism. To evaluate each learning model, we use 800 subjects (70%) for model training and 311 subjects (30%) for hold-out testing. We use the same case/control ratio (0.5157) for both training and test set."

Preprocessing software (SPM8) and steps are described by reference to a prior paper's pipeline, but no atlas/parcellation is used (features are ICA spatial components and texture filters) and no CPAC/DPARSF pipeline version is reported.
Diagnosis source is not described in this paper beyond citing the ABIDE release.

Hyperparameters were selected via 5-fold CV restricted to the training set only, with a held-out test set reserved for final evaluation, and an explicit site-confound check (site-only baseline accuracy near chance; site-balanced test sets gave similar accuracy to the original): "We then tested those previously-trained classifiers on these new “site-balanced test sets” and found that the accuracies did not differ significantly from the original test set results: here, it was 69.88% for ADHD-200 and 63.46% for ABIDE."

risk_of_bias.summary: Cohort, train/test split and site-confound checks are all explicit and leakage-conscious (CV confined to training data, a site-balanced test replication); the main gaps are the absence of a named atlas/standard connectivity pipeline and an undescribed diagnostic label source.

narrative_row.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction (SVM on combined structural-texture and functional-ICA features) using ABIDE I (1111 scans, 573 HC/538 ASD, 17 sites), split 800 training / 311 hold-out test (case:control ratio preserved).
narrative_row.methods: SPM8-preprocessed structural and resting-state fMRI; structural texture features from a sparse-autoencoder convolutional model and functional features from subject-level spatial ICA time courses, combined via linear SVM (LEFMSF); 5-fold CV for hyperparameter tuning within the training set, evaluated on an untouched hold-out set; explicit site-confound checks.
narrative_row.outcomes: LEFMSF achieved 0.643 hold-out accuracy on ABIDE (specificity 0.683, sensitivity 0.600), the best known result using imaging data alone at publication, exceeding prior work by 0.042; a site-only baseline classifier scored only 55.0% and a site-balanced re-test gave 63.46%, arguing against a site-driven result.
narrative_row.key_limitations: No named ROI atlas/standard connectivity pipeline (features are ICA/texture-based); no motion/FD-based QC rule reported; diagnostic label source not described; exact ASD/TD counts within the hold-out test set not individually reported.
narrative_row.relevance_notes: A methodologically careful example combining structural and functional ABIDE I features with an explicit, quantitative check that model performance is not driven by site identity, directly relevant to confound/leakage assessment in ABIDE-based prediction studies.

screening.reason: Reports a deep-transfer-learning diagnostic prediction (ASD vs. control) analysis of ABIDE resting-state fMRI functional connectivity across four ABIDE sites, with offline pretraining on the remaining ABIDE sites (Inclusion 2, 3).

evidence_spans.text: we compared the performance of our DTL-NN approach with a traditional deep neural network and support vector machine models across four ABIDE data sites that enrolled at least 60 subjects. As compared to traditional models, our DTL-NN approach achieved an improved performance in accuracy, sensitivity, speciﬁcity and area under receiver operating characteristic curve.
evidence_spans.claim: DTL-NN was compared with a traditional DNN and SVM for ASD classification across four ABIDE sites with at least 60 subjects, achieving improved accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC.

evidence_spans.text: The rs- fMRI data were processed using Connectome Computation System (Xu et al., 2015) pipeline, which includes slice timing correction, motion realignment, and intensity normalization. Nuisance variable regression (Fox et al., 2005; Lund et al., 2005) was implemented through band-pass ﬁltering and global signal regression strategies to clean confounding variations introduced by heartbeats and respirations, head motion, and low frequency scanner drifts. Furthermore, boundary-based rigid body and FMRIB’s linear & nonlinear image registration tools (Andersson et al., 2008; Ratziu et al., 2008) were used to register functional to anatomical images. Then, both functional and anatomical images were normalized to a standard template space, the Automated Anatomical Labeling atlas (Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2002).
evidence_spans.claim: Data were preprocessed with the Connectome Computation System pipeline and parcellated with the AAL atlas into a 90x90 functional connectivity matrix.

evidence_spans.text: Site bias was corrected among diﬀerent sites similar to an approach described previously by an ABIDE study (Heinsfeld et al., 2018). Speciﬁcally, a multiple regression analysis was conducted to control for potentially confounding variables (site, age, gender, and handedness). These variables were regressed from FC weights across connections among ROIs. When adjusting for the confounding factors, our regression model is: y = β0 + β1x1 + β2x2 + β3x3 + β4x4 + ε where y is the vector of FC weights, x1 to x4 represent the four explanatory variables, site, age, gender, and handedness. βi is the intercept and the corresponding regression coeﬃcients. ε is the residual vector. Using ordinary least squares (OLS) estimation, βi was estimated. Then, these cofounding variables were regressed out from the FC weights.
evidence_spans.claim: Site, age, gender and handedness were regressed out of FC weights via OLS multiple regression to correct for site bias.

evidence_spans.text: we performed ASD classiﬁcation experiments on four individual data sites with at least 60 subjects, including University of Michigan (UM), University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), University of Utah School of Medicine (USM), and Katholieke Universiteit Leuven (LEUVEN).
evidence_spans.claim: ASD classification experiments were performed on four individual ABIDE sites with at least 60 subjects: UM, UCLA, USM and LEUVEN.

evidence_spans.text: the independent healthy FC data from the remaining 16 sites from the ABIDE repository were accumulated as pre- collected data to train an SSAE prototype during oﬄine learning. Then, we randomly split the data from the target site into training and testing set. The data from the training set were applied on an SSAE prototype in the prior knowledge aided training step. The hold-out testing data were then used to evaluate the trained DTL-NN model.
evidence_spans.claim: The offline SSAE prototype was pretrained on healthy subjects pooled from the 16 remaining (non-target) ABIDE sites, keeping the target site's data separate for training/testing.

narrative_row.methods: CCS-preprocessed functional connectivity (AAL atlas, 90 ROIs) with site/age/gender/handedness regressed out via OLS; a stacked sparse autoencoder pretrained offline on non-target-site healthy subjects, transferred into a DTL-NN classifier and compared against DNN and SVM baselines via stratified 5-fold CV per site.
narrative_row.outcomes: DTL-NN outperformed DNN and SVM at every site, with the best performance at USM (70.4% accuracy, 0.73 AUC) and an average of 67.1% accuracy/0.71 AUC across sites, significantly better than DNN for accuracy (p=0.03) and sensitivity (p=0.04).
narrative_row.key_limitations: No motion/FD-based QC threshold or pipeline version reported; diagnostic label source not described; no code/participant-list availability statement; small per-site sample sizes (61-113).
narrative_row.relevance_notes: Demonstrates a transfer-learning design that explicitly separates offline pretraining data (non-target ABIDE sites) from target-site evaluation data, alongside an explicit site-covariate regression, both directly relevant to site-leakage assessment in ABIDE-based prediction studies.

Only 84 of 107 subjects are utilized in experiments because the translation or rotation of 7 TC and 16 ASD patients has surpassed ±2 mm or ±2◦.

evidence_spans.text: Only 84 of 107 subjects are utilized in experiments because the translation or rotation of 7 TC and 16 ASD patients has surpassed ±2 mm or ±2◦. Then the random SVM cluster was proposed to distinguish TC and ASD. The results show that this method has an excellent classiﬁcation performance based on all the features. Furthermore, the accuracy based on the optimal feature set could reach to 96.15%. Abnormal brain regions could also be found, such as inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (orbital and opercula part), hippocampus, and precuneus. It is indicated that the method of random SVM cluster may apply to the auxiliary diagnosis of ASD. Keywords: random support vector machine cluster, neuroimaging, autism spectrum disorder, classiﬁcation, feature selection INTRODUCTION Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is mainly reﬂected in the communication and language barriers, diﬃculties in social communication, and it is a kind of neurological developmental disorder (Karten and Hirsch, 2015; Khundrakpam et al., 2017). The behavioral phenotype of ASD is well-depicted but its etiology and pathogenesis is rarely known (Amaral et al., 2008). According to the results of Hallmayer et al. (2011), the causes of ASD mainly include genetic and environmental risk factors. Some of the symptoms of ASD generally appear in about 2 years old (Ecker et al., 2015), thus the early diagnosis is needed (Plitt et al., 2015). It is recognized that traditional clinical methods cannot well distinguish patients from healthy controls (HC) (Mwangi et al., 2012). And it may not be complex enough to capture the abnormal brain regions in individuals who suﬀering from ASD (Uddin et al., 2011). To avoid this disadvantage, machine learning is introduced in the neuroimaging ﬁeld. It is a valid means to extract messages from neuroimaging data and further predict the future changes of the disease (Klöppel et al., 2012; Orrù et al., 2012). Among numerous machine learning methods, support vector machines (SVM) is an excellent classiﬁcation method Bi et al. Classiﬁcation of ASD Using Random-SVM-Cluster (Zhang et al., 2015). SVM has distinct merits such as the higher classiﬁcation accuracy (Zhang and Wu, 2012) and no need for a large number of training samples to avoid over-ﬁtting (Li et al., 2010). Thus, SVM has aroused widespread concern of researchers in the ﬁeld of neuroimaging (Sundermann et al., 2014). In the researches of machine learning, SVM has been applied to classify ASD from corresponding controls. Gori et al. (2015) extracted features from the gray matter subregions, then these features were used in SVM to identity ASD from HC and the area under ROC curve (AUC) is 0.74. Jin et al. (2015) proposed an original multi-kernel SVM classiﬁcation method to classify ASD from HC and the accuracy can reach to 76%. Chen et al. (2016) used the SVM to classify 112 adolescent subjects with ASD and 128 HC, and the classiﬁcation accuracy was 79.17%. Odriozola et al. (2015) used the SVM based on functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data to classify 20 children with ASD and 20 typically developing (TD) peers, and the result showed 85% classiﬁcation accuracy. Chanel et al. (2016) used the method of SVM and Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) based on fMRI data to classify ASD from HC, and the result showed good classiﬁcation accuracy (up to 92.3%). These SVM classiﬁcation studies on ASD have achieved relatively high classiﬁcation accuracy in the range of 70–93% compared with traditional methods. They usually employed a single SVM and common features such as functional connections, gray matter volume to classify ASD from HC, and the classiﬁcation accuracy is generally lower than 90%. In this paper, a novel method of random SVM cluster is proposed and several graph metrics of brain functional connectivity (e.g., local eﬃciency, shortest path) are employed to classify ASD and typical controls (TC). This method has some good performance. Firstly, the classiﬁcation accuracy reaches to a higher level based on all the features. Then, we could ﬁnd out the optimal feature set, the classiﬁcation accuracy could also reach to the same level based on the optimal feature set. Thirdly, on the basis of the optimal feature set, we could ﬁnd out the abnormal brain regions such as inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (orbital and opercula part), hippocampus, and precuneus. Thus, the random SVM cluster may apply to the auxiliary diagnosis of ASD. MATERIALS AND METHODS Demographic Information The Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) database (http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/abide/) (Di Martino et al., 2014) contains a variety of neuroimaging data. And the resting-state fMRI data include 539 ASD and 573 age-matched TC. There are 12 kinds of image protocols. This study chooses one of the image protocols, details as follows. MRI scanner = 3.0- T Siemens, TR = 3,000 ms, TE = 28 ms, data matrix = 64∗64, Pixel Spacing X = 3.0 mm, Pixel Spacing Y = 3.0 mm, Flip Angle = 90◦, Slice Thickness = 0.0 mm, no slice gap, axial slices = 34, time points = 120. Finally, 61 subjects with ASD and 46 TC met the image protocol. The original studies included in ABIDE received approval from each site’s Institutional Review Board (IRB). All images were obtained with informed consent according to procedures established by human subject research boards. Only 84 of 107 subjects are utilized in experiments because the translation or the rotation of 7 TC and 16 ASD patients has surpassed ± 2 mm or ± 2◦.

evidence_spans.text: all the fMRI images are preprocessed by the Data Processing Assistant for Resting- State fMRI (DPARSF) software (Cui et al., 2015) (http://d.rnet. co/DPABI/DPABI_V2.3_170105.zip). The whole preprocessing procedures include:(1) Converting DICOM to NIFTI, (2) Removing the ﬁrst 10 time points, (3) Slicing timing, (4) Realigning, (5) Normalizing with the echo-planar imaging (EPI) template, (6) Smoothing, (7) Removing the linear trend, (8) Temporal ﬁltering, (9) Removing covariates.
evidence_spans.claim: All fMRI images were preprocessed using DPARSF software.

evidence_spans.text: fMRI image could be divided into 90 regions based on the Automatic Anatomical Labeling (AAL) (Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2002) atlas. We make these regions as the nodes of brain network, so there are 90 nodes. An average of the time series of a region’s all voxels can be used to capture the mean time series of this region (Khazaee et al., 2016). The average time series of every two brain regions can be employed to calculate the Pearson correlation coeﬃcient which is made as the link of the brain network (Khazaee et al., 2015), so there are 4,005 (90∗89/2) weighted edges.
evidence_spans.claim: The brain was parcellated into 90 regions using the AAL atlas, yielding 4,005 pairwise connectivity edges.

evidence_spans.text: Firstly, the 84 samples are divided into 58 training samples and 26 test samples based on the ratio of 7:3. Then 50 samples are randomly selected from the 58 training samples and 62 features are randomly selected from 4,225 features, which form a single SVM using Radial Basis Function (RBF) as kernel provided by the SVM toolbox (http://see.xidian.edu.cn/faculty/chzheng/ bishe/indexﬁles/indexl.htm) (Gunn, 1998). The width argument of RBF equals to 3, and penalty coeﬃcient equals to Inf. The process is repeated for 500 times and these 500 SVMs constitute into a random SVM cluster.
evidence_spans.claim: The 84 samples were split once into 58 training and 26 test samples (ratio 7:3) to build and evaluate the random SVM cluster.

evidence_spans.text: the accuracy of the random SVM cluster is as high as 96.15%. This is suﬃcient to show that the performance of the random SVM cluster is much better than a single SVM.
evidence_spans.claim: The random SVM cluster achieved 96.15% accuracy, much higher than a single SVM.

Keywords: random support vector machine cluster, neuroimaging, autism spectrum disorder, classiﬁcation, feature selection INTRODUCTION Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is mainly reﬂected in the communication and language barriers, diﬃculties in social communication, and it is a kind of neurological developmental disorder (Karten and Hirsch, 2015; Khundrakpam et al., 2017). The behavioral phenotype of ASD is well-depicted but its etiology and pathogenesis is rarely known (Amaral et al., 2008). According to the results of Hallmayer et al. (2011), the causes of ASD mainly include genetic and environmental risk factors. Some of the symptoms of ASD generally appear in about 2 years old (Ecker et al., 2015), thus the early diagnosis is needed (Plitt et al., 2015). It is recognized that traditional clinical methods cannot well distinguish patients from healthy controls (HC) (Mwangi et al., 2012). And it may not be complex enough to capture the abnormal brain regions in individuals who suﬀering from ASD (Uddin et al., 2011). To avoid this disadvantage, machine learning is introduced in the neuroimaging ﬁeld. It is a valid means to extract messages from neuroimaging data and further predict the future changes of the disease (Klöppel et al., 2012; Orrù et al., 2012). Among numerous machine learning methods, support vector machines (SVM) is an excellent classiﬁcation method Bi et al. Classiﬁcation of ASD Using Random-SVM-Cluster (Zhang et al., 2015). SVM has distinct merits such as the higher classiﬁcation accuracy (Zhang and Wu, 2012) and no need for a large number of training samples to avoid over-ﬁtting (Li et al., 2010). Thus, SVM has aroused widespread concern of researchers in the ﬁeld of neuroimaging (Sundermann et al., 2014). In the researches of machine learning, SVM has been applied to classify ASD from corresponding controls. Gori et al. (2015) extracted features from the gray matter subregions, then these features were used in SVM to identity ASD from HC and the area under ROC curve (AUC) is 0.74. Jin et al. (2015) proposed an original multi-kernel SVM classiﬁcation method to classify ASD from HC and the accuracy can reach to 76%. Chen et al. (2016) used the SVM to classify 112 adolescent subjects with ASD and 128 HC, and the classiﬁcation accuracy was 79.17%. Odriozola et al. (2015) used the SVM based on functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data to classify 20 children with ASD and 20 typically developing (TD) peers, and the result showed 85% classiﬁcation accuracy. Chanel et al. (2016) used the method of SVM and Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) based on fMRI data to classify ASD from HC, and the result showed good classiﬁcation accuracy (up to 92.3%). These SVM classiﬁcation studies on ASD have achieved relatively high classiﬁcation accuracy in the range of 70–93% compared with traditional methods. They usually employed a single SVM and common features such as functional connections, gray matter volume to classify ASD from HC, and the classiﬁcation accuracy is generally lower than 90%. In this paper, a novel method of random SVM cluster is proposed and several graph metrics of brain functional connectivity (e.g., local eﬃciency, shortest path) are employed to classify ASD and typical controls (TC). This method has some good performance. Firstly, the classiﬁcation accuracy reaches to a higher level based on all the features. Then, we could ﬁnd out the optimal feature set, the classiﬁcation accuracy could also reach to the same level based on the optimal feature set. Thirdly, on the basis of the optimal feature set, we could ﬁnd out the abnormal brain regions such as inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) (orbital and opercula part), hippocampus, and precuneus. Thus, the random SVM cluster may apply to the auxiliary diagnosis of ASD. MATERIALS AND METHODS Demographic Information The Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) database (http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/abide/) (Di Martino et al., 2014) contains a variety of neuroimaging data. And the resting-state fMRI data include 539 ASD and 573 age-matched TC. There are 12 kinds of image protocols. This study chooses one of the image protocols, details as follows. MRI scanner = 3.0- T Siemens, TR = 3,000 ms, TE = 28 ms, data matrix = 64∗64, Pixel Spacing X = 3.0 mm, Pixel Spacing Y = 3.0 mm, Flip Angle = 90◦, Slice Thickness = 0.0 mm, no slice gap, axial slices = 34, time points = 120. Finally, 61 subjects with ASD and 46 TC met the image protocol. The original studies included in ABIDE received approval from each site’s Institutional Review Board (IRB). All images were obtained with informed consent according to procedures established by human subject research boards. Only 84 of 107 subjects are utilized in experiments because the translation or the rotation of 7 TC and 16 ASD patients has surpassed ± 2 mm or ± 2◦."

screening.reason: Reports a diagnostic prediction (ASD vs. control) analysis of combined ABIDE I+II resting-state fMRI using 3D-CNNs on temporal summary measures, with both 5-fold and leave-site-out cross-validation (Inclusion 2, 3).

evidence_spans.text: We attained results competitive on this task for a combined ABIDE-I and II datasets of ~66%. When all summary measures were combined the result was still only as good as that of the best single measure which was regional homogeneity (ReHo).
evidence_spans.claim: The 3D-CNN achieved ~66% accuracy on the combined ABIDE I+II dataset; combining all summary measures performed no better than the best single measure (ReHo).

evidence_spans.text: The ABIDE I+II datasets is a collection of structural (T1w) and functional (rs-fMRI) brain images aggregated across 29 institutions (10), available for download2. It includes 1,028 participants with a diagnosis of autism, Asperger or pervasive developmental disorder-not otherwise speciﬁed (called ASD from now on), and 1,141 typically developing participants (CON).
evidence_spans.claim: ABIDE I+II aggregates data from 29 institutions, with 1,028 ASD and 1,141 typically developing participants in the full release.

evidence_spans.text: We chose to cut off the minimum scan duration to 100-time points, which led us to include 96% of the whole ABIDE I+II dataset (N=2,085, N(ASD) =993), the vast majority of which (95%) with a minimum acquisition time of 4 min.
evidence_spans.claim: A minimum scan-duration cutoff of 100 time points retained 96% of ABIDE I+II (N=2,085, N(ASD)=993).

evidence_spans.text: The preprocessing was done using the Conﬁgurable Pipeline for the Analysis of Connectomes (C-PAC, (12). We followed a preprocessing strategy adopted by the Preprocessed Connectome Project initiative3. This will allow others to replicate and extend the ﬁndings in this paper.
evidence_spans.claim: Preprocessing used C-PAC following a Preprocessed Connectomes Project strategy, chosen explicitly to enable replication.

evidence_spans.text: For the leave-site-out CV procedure, we selected ﬁve sites with the highest number of total subjects (ASD/total), namely New York University (NYU) (90/159), Kennedy Krieger Institute - 1 (KKI-I) (88/114), University of Miami - 1 (UM-I) (50/96), University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)-I (28/69), Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU)-I (42/64).
evidence_spans.claim: The leave-site-out evaluation used the five largest sites (NYU, KKI-I, UM-I, UCLA-I, OHSU-I) with each held out as the test set in turn.

evidence_spans.text: When assessed by ﬁve-fold CV procedure, all tested models performed at around 60% accuracy for the classiﬁcation task (Figure 2 and Table 2), with little variation between models' performances. On the contrary, the leave-site-out CV procedure shows high variability in terms of model performances with relatively good performance for the NYU site and poor performance for the other sites
evidence_spans.claim: Five-fold CV gave around 60% accuracy for all models with little variation, while leave-site-out CV showed high variability, good for NYU and poor for other sites.

evidence_spans.text: The overall best performing model was the MM-ensemble, which achieved balanced accuracy of 64% and F1 score of 66%, averaged over the ﬁve-folds of the CV procedure. evidence_spans.text: In this study, we used the fMRI data of 816 individuals enrolled in the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) to introduce a new biomarker extraction pipeline for ASD that relies on the use of graph theoretical metrics of fMRI-based functional connectivity to inform a support vector machine (SVM).
evidence_spans.claim: The study used fMRI data of 816 ABIDE individuals, extracting graph-theoretical metrics of functional connectivity to inform an SVM classifier.

evidence_spans.text: Our methodology achieved better results than most state-of-the-art investigations on this dataset with the best model for the >30 years age group achieving an accuracy, sensitivity, and speciﬁcity of 95, 97, and 95%, respectively.

Regions of interests (ROIs) were deﬁned as the 116 regions in the automatic anatomical labeling (AAL) atlas (Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2002).

charting.feature_extraction_tools: PANDA toolbox used as the comparison baseline for brain-network construction on ABIDE; the proposed DGCL (diffusion-based brain-region alignment module + graph-contrastive brain-network optimization module) used as the main method; ABIDE-specific preprocessing pipeline not otherwise described
charting.importance_method: ROI attention/cue-vector scores from the learned brain-network matrix
charting.top_features_identified: Somatomotor network (SMN) connectivity, and DMN-DAN / DMN-FPN connectivity

charting.model_category: Diffusion-based generative brain-network construction (Dual U-Net denoising/registration) + graph convolutional network classifier with graph-contrastive brain-network optimization
charting.specific_algorithms: DGCL: Brain Region Alignment Module (BRAM, DDPM-based) and Brain Network Optimization Module (BNOM, GCN-based graph contrastive learning), compared against a PANDA-constructed network + GCN/MLP baseline
charting.validation_methodology: Five-fold cross-validation (stated generically for "the model"; no ABIDE-specific validation detail given)
charting.performance_metrics: Accuracy (ACC), sensitivity (SEN), specificity (SPE), AUC (metrics defined for the overall evaluation; ICC reliability also reported for ABIDE network construction)

assessments.support: N by diagnosis (506 ASD/548 TC) and site count (17) reported, but the only exclusion rule stated is "excluded subjects whose imaging data shows some missing" with no motion/QC threshold.
C-PAC pipeline with nuisance regression, band-pass filtering and ANTs normalization is described, and CC200 atlas connectivity is the feature basis.
ASD vs TC labels used without stating the diagnostic instrument/source.

The top 1935 features are described as selected before the 10-fold CV procedure is introduced, suggesting feature selection may not have been confined to training folds; the pooled 10-fold CV does not account for site, though a separate intra-site stratified shuffle-split analysis was also run (lower accuracy, 67.7%, suggesting some site-driven inflation in the pooled result).

risk_of_bias.summary: Cohort size, sites and pipeline (C-PAC, CC200) are well reported, but the exclusion rule is minimal (missing data only, no motion threshold), diagnosis source is not stated, and the description of feature selection preceding cross-validation raises a leakage concern; a supplementary intra-site evaluation showed lower accuracy than the pooled 10-fold result, consistent with some site leakage in the main result.
