screening.reason: Reports a 3-D CNN diagnostic classification of ASD vs NC using resting-state fMRI brain functional networks from the ABIDE-I NYU site (Inclusion 2, 3)

evidence_spans.text:
Results: We collected 79 ASD patients and 105 NCs from the ABIDE-I dataset.
The mean accuracy of our classiﬁcation algorithm was 77.74% for classiﬁcation
of ASD versus NCs.
evidence_spans.claim: A 3-D CNN classifying ASD vs NC from 79 ASD and 105 NC ABIDE-I subjects achieved 77.74% mean accuracy.

evidence_spans.text:
The ﬁrst phase of ABIDE (ABIDE-I)
compiles a dataset of 1112 individuals from 17 sites and
consists of 539 individuals with ASD and 573 typical controls. 
Since the scan parameters vary across sites, ABIDE is a highly
heterogeneous dataset. To avoid the impact of data heterogeneity,
we collected raw rs-fMRI data from the whole NYU site,
consisting of 79 ASD subjects and 105 normal controls (NCs).
evidence_spans.claim: To avoid cross-site heterogeneity, the study restricted analysis to the single NYU site of ABIDE-I (79 ASD, 105 NC) rather than the full 539/573 ABIDE-I sample.

evidence_spans.text:
We preprocessed the data using a widely adopted pipeline called
Conﬁgurable Pipeline for the Analysis of Connectomes (C-PAC)
(Craddock et al., 2013), which involves skull striping, slice timing
correction, realignment to correct for motion, and bandpass
ﬁltering (0.01–0.1 Hz).
evidence_spans.claim: Data were preprocessed with C-PAC (skull stripping, slice timing, motion realignment, bandpass filtering).

components were derived using Group-ICA, and further inspected to identify eight well deﬁned brain function networks (BFNs). (B) The selected BFNs were used to
extract subject-speciﬁc spatial maps using dual regression.
evidence_spans.claim: Eight brain functional networks were derived via group-ICA and subject-specific maps via dual regression, used as 3-D CNN input.

evidence_spans.text:
A total of 10-fold cross validation strategy was used for evaluating classiﬁcation
performance.
evidence_spans.claim: Classification performance was evaluated with 10-fold cross-validation.

evidence_spans.text:
The SN-dDMN and SN-LCEN pairs showed
increased connectivity strength in ASD, and hypo-connectivity
was observed in the PCUN-dDMN pair of ASD.
evidence_spans.claim: ASD showed hyperconnectivity between salience network (SN) and dorsal DMN, and between SN and left central executive network, and hypoconnectivity between precuneus and dorsal DMN.

evidence_spans.text:
Our ﬁndings support the under-connectivity hypnosis in
autism proposed by Just et al. (2004).
evidence_spans.claim: Findings are interpreted as supporting the under-connectivity hypothesis of autism.

assessments.support: N by diagnosis (79 ASD/105 NC), single site (NYU), and demographics (age, IQ, ADOS) are reported in Table 1; restriction to one site is explicitly justified as avoiding cross-site heterogeneity.
C-PAC pipeline, group-ICA-derived BFNs and dual regression are described in detail.

ADOS total/communication/social scores reported for the ASD group as part of Table 1, indicating ADOS-based diagnosis, though the exact diagnostic criterion/instrument sentence is not quoted verbatim.

Group-ICA and dual regression appear to have been performed on the full sample before the random train/validation split and 10-fold cross-validation, with no stated leakage control; no uncertainty interval is given around the single reported accuracy; site handling is not applicable (single site) but this also means findings are not tested for cross-site generalization.

risk_of_bias.summary: Cohort, pipeline and demographic/clinical reporting are thorough for this single-site (NYU) ABIDE-I subsample, but group-ICA/dual-regression feature derivation appears to precede the cross-validation split with no stated leakage control, and the single reported accuracy lacks an uncertainty interval; the deliberate single-site design avoids cross-site heterogeneity but means no site-generalization evidence is provided.

narrative_row.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction (ASD vs NC); ABIDE-I, single NYU site only, 79 ASD / 105 NC (full ABIDE-I: 539 ASD/573 TC across 17 sites)
narrative_row.methods: C-PAC-preprocessed rs-fMRI; group-ICA identified eight brain functional networks, subject-specific spatial maps via dual regression, classified with a modified 3-D VGG-Net with squeeze-and-excitation channel attention (MCSE-VGG); evaluated with 10-fold cross-validation.
narrative_row.outcomes: MCSE-VGG achieved 77.74% accuracy (76.74% precision, 78.57% recall, F1 75.33%) versus a 69.58%-accuracy baseline; ASD showed hyperconnectivity between the salience network and DMN/central executive network and hypoconnectivity between precuneus and dorsal DMN, consistent with the under-connectivity hypothesis.
narrative_row.key_limitations: Single-site design chosen to avoid cross-site heterogeneity, so no cross-site generalization evidence; no separate validation dataset; ASD and NC groups differed significantly in age and IQ; no motion/QC threshold or leakage-control statement; no code/participant list released.
narrative_row.relevance_notes: A well-documented single-site ABIDE-I predictive study illustrating a deliberate site-restriction strategy as an alternative to multi-site harmonisation.

evidence_spans.text:
The Autism Brain Imaging Data Ex-
change (ABIDE)1 [39] initiative aggregates resting-state
functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) and phe-
notypic data of 1112 subjects from various international
brain imaging laboratories. We select a set of 871 subjects,
consisting of 403 ASD patients and 468 healthy controls
(HCs).
evidence_spans.claim: Cohort was 871 of 1112 ABIDE subjects (403 ASD, 468 HC).

evidence_spans.text:
For preprocessing of
the ABIDE dataset, we use the Configurable Pipeline for the
Analysis of Connectomes (C-PAC) [41], which includes skull
stripping, slice timing correction, motion correction, global
mean intensity normalization, nuisance signal regression, band-
pass filtering (0.01-0.1Hz), and registration of fMRI images to a
standard anatomical space. Then, the mean timeseries for a set
of cortical and subcortical regions of interest (ROIs) extracted
from the Har
evidence_spans.claim: ABIDE data preprocessed with C-PAC and parcellated with the Harvard-Oxford atlas.

evidence_spans.text:
For the edge weights of the population graph
on the ABIDE datset, we incorporate the subject’s gender, age
and acquisition site as as phenotypic measures.
evidence_spans.claim: Site, age and gender are used as phenotypic edge-weight features in the population graph used for node classification.

evidence_spans.text: We use a stratified 10-fold cross-validation strategy.
evidence_spans.claim: Model evaluated with stratified 10-fold cross-validation.
Baseline GCN achieved 64.63% accuracy / 72.23% AUC on ABIDE.
The proposed AN-GCN achieved 96.91% accuracy and 96.86% AUC on ABIDE, far exceeding all baselines (best baseline DS-MML: 87.62% accuracy, 92.00% AUC).

evidence_spans.text:
the results show that our model outperforms all the base-
line methods on the ABIDE dataset, achieving relative improve-
ments of 50.33%, 34.10%, 50.33%, 12.25% and 50.33% over
GCN in terms of accuracy, AUC, F1-score, recall and precision,
respectively.
evidence_spans.claim: AN-GCN improved relative accuracy by 50.33% over the baseline GCN on ABIDE.

evidence_spans.text:
Hence, we take the upper triangular
part and vectorize it to obtain a feature vector whose dimension
is then further reduced using recursive feature elimination via a
ridge classifier.
evidence_spans.claim: Connectivity feature vectors are dimensionality-reduced via recursive feature elimination with a ridge classifier before the 10-fold CV procedure is described, with no statement that this is confined to training folds.

assessments.support: N by diagnosis (403 ASD/468 HC of 871 selected from 1112) is reported, though the exact selection/exclusion rule for the 871 is not detailed beyond "we select a set of 871 subjects".
C-PAC pipeline and Harvard-Oxford atlas are described in detail, with Fisher z-transformed Pearson correlation connectivity features.
ASD vs HC labels used without stating the diagnostic instrument/source.

Recursive feature elimination via a ridge classifier is described prior to the cross-validation section with no statement that it is confined to training folds; the population graph is built transductively using phenotypic data (including site) from all subjects before node classification; site is used as a graph-edge similarity feature rather than being held out or corrected for, and no leave-site-out evaluation is reported. The reported accuracy (96.91%) is far above both the baselines in this paper (best baseline 87.62%) and most published ABIDE benchmarks, consistent with a leakage-driven inflation.

risk_of_bias.summary: Cohort size and pipeline/atlas are well reported, but feature reduction (recursive feature elimination) appears to precede the stratified 10-fold cross-validation with no stated leakage control, the transductive population graph is built using all subjects' phenotypic data (including site) before fold assignment, and no leave-site-out check is reported; the resulting accuracy (96.91%) is implausibly high relative to the paper's own baselines and the published ABIDE literature, consistent with a leakage-driven result.

charting.key_performance_results: AN-GCN: 96.91% accuracy, 96.86% AUC, 97.16% F1, 96.91% recall, 97.00% precision on ABIDE, versus the strongest baseline DS-MML (87.62% accuracy, 92.00% AUC) and baseline GCN (64.63% accuracy, 72.23% AUC); a relative improvement of 50.33% in accuracy over GCN
charting.summary_key_findings: A population-graph GCN with skip connections and identity mapping (AN-GCN) classified ASD vs HC on 871 ABIDE subjects (403 ASD/468 HC) with 96.91% accuracy and 96.86% AUC, substantially exceeding all compared baselines including a strong recent method (DS-MML, 87.62% accuracy); feature reduction (recursive feature elimination) is described prior to the cross-validation step and site/age/gender are embedded directly as population-graph edge weights, raising a leakage/inflation concern given this result is far above both the paper's own baselines and typical published ABIDE benchmarks.
charting.reviewer_notes: Reported 96.91% accuracy is markedly higher than the paper's own strongest baseline (87.62%) and most published ABIDE classification results, consistent with the leakage risk noted (feature elimination preceding CV; transductive population graph using site/age/gender from all subjects).

narrative_row.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction (ASD vs HC); ABIDE (consistent with ABIDE I), 871 of 1112 subjects (403 ASD, 468 HC)
narrative_row.methods: C-PAC-preprocessed rs-fMRI parcellated with the Harvard-Oxford atlas; Fisher z-transformed Pearson connectivity, dimensionality-reduced via recursive feature elimination; a transductive population graph (nodes = imaging features, edges weighted by gender/age/acquisition site) classified with a proposed attention/skip-connection GCN (AN-GCN), evaluated with stratified 10-fold cross-validation against several GCN-based baselines.
narrative_row.outcomes: AN-GCN achieved 96.91% accuracy and 96.86% AUC on ABIDE, far exceeding the strongest compared baseline (DS-MML, 87.62% accuracy, 92.00% AUC) and the basic GCN baseline (64.63% accuracy).
narrative_row.key_limitations: No diagnosis-source statement; feature elimination appears to precede the CV split; site/age/gender used directly as population-graph edge weights rather than controlled for, with no leave-site-out evaluation; the very high accuracy is substantially above the paper's own baselines and typical ABIDE benchmarks, suggesting possible leakage/inflation.
narrative_row.relevance_notes: Illustrates a predictive, transductive population-graph GCN approach on ABIDE with a pipeline/atlas clearly reported but validation design raising leakage concerns given an unusually high accuracy.

evidence_spans.text: We select the same set of 871 subjects used by Abraham et al. (2017) that met the imaging quality and phenotypic information criteria, comprising 403 individuals with ASD and 468 healthy controls. These subjects were regrouped based on location into 20 imaging sites.
evidence_spans.claim: Cohort is the same 871-subject ABIDE I subset (403 ASD, 468 controls) as Abraham et al. 2017, from 20 sites.

evidence_spans.text: we use the same preprocessing pipeline, the Conﬁgurable Pipeline for the Analysis of Connectomes (C-PAC) (Craddock et al., 2013), which involves skull striping, slice timing correction, motion correction, global mean intensity normalisation, nuisance signal regression, band-pass ﬁltering (0.01- 0.1Hz)
evidence_spans.claim: Preprocessing used C-PAC (skull stripping, motion correction, nuisance regression, band-pass filtering 0.01-0.1Hz).

evidence_spans.text: the mean time series for a set of regions extracted from the Harvard Oxford (HO) atlas (Desikan et al., 2006) were computed and normalised to zero mean and unit variance
evidence_spans.claim: Harvard-Oxford atlas used for ROI time-series extraction and connectivity feature construction.

evidence_spans.text: We evaluate our model on both the ADNI and ABIDE databases using a 10-fold stratiﬁed cross validation strategy.
evidence_spans.claim: Evaluation used 10-fold stratified cross-validation (not leave-site-out).

evidence_spans.text: We focus our attention to the phenotypic graph (using default phenotypic measures), which corresponds to the graph constructed taking into account SEX and SITE information, weighted by the feature correlation similarity.
evidence_spans.claim: The best-performing population graph uses sex and site as phenotypic edge-weighting measures alongside imaging feature similarity.

evidence_spans.text: In Parisot et al. (2017), we used a ridge classiﬁer to perform Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) with a ﬁxed number of features C. It is an iterative process, where each iteration trains the ridge classiﬁer on the training set with the current feature vector.
evidence_spans.claim: Feature selection (RFE) was trained on the training set within the cross-validation scheme.

evidence_spans.text: The best average performance is achieved for K = 4 with accuracy 70.4% and AUC 0.75.
evidence_spans.claim: Best GCN classification result on ABIDE: 70.4% accuracy, AUC 0.75, with a K=4 Chebyshev polynomial order on the phenotypic graph.

evidence_spans.text: Our experiments suggest that an accuracy of approx. 70% could be an intrinsic limitation of the whole dataset.
evidence_spans.claim: Authors interpret the ~70% accuracy ceiling as a possible intrinsic limitation of the heterogeneous multi-site ABIDE dataset.

assessments.support: Reuses the well-documented 871-subject (403 ASD/468 control), 20-site ABIDE I subset from Abraham et al. 2017.
Harvard-Oxford atlas, C-PAC pipeline, and multiple feature-selection strategies (RFE, PCA, MLP, autoencoder) explicitly described and compared.
Diagnostic label (ASD vs control) inherited from ABIDE phenotypic file; no specific diagnostic instrument/criteria stated in this paper.

Evaluation uses 10-fold stratified CV (not site-held-out) despite site being a known confound, and the GCN is semi-supervised/transductive: unlabelled test-node imaging features and phenotypic edges are present in the graph during training, even though RFE itself is fit on training folds only.

risk_of_bias.summary: Methodologically transparent predictive GCN study on a well-characterised ABIDE subset, but site-stratified (not site-held-out) CV and transductive graph construction leave open whether reported accuracy generalises to unseen sites.

evidence_spans.text: We attempted to replicate the method and results using the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) including resting state fMRI data obtained from 964 subjects and 16 separate international sites.
evidence_spans.claim: Study replicates a single-site connectivity classification approach on a 964-subject, 16-site ABIDE sample.

evidence_spans.text: A total of 964 subjects met all inclusion criteria (517 typically developing subjects and 447 subjects with autism from 16 sites).
evidence_spans.claim: Analysed cohort: 964 ABIDE I participants (447 autism, 517 typically developing) from 16 sites after applying inclusion criteria.

evidence_spans.text: Inclusion criteria for subjects were successful preprocessing with manual visual inspection of normalization to MNI space of MPRAGE, coregistration of BOLD and MPRAGE images, seg- mentation of MPRAG
evidence_spans.claim: QC rule was manual visual inspection of normalization/coregistration/segmentation success, not a numeric motion threshold at the subject-inclusion stage.

evidence_spans.text: Motion scrubbing (Power et al., 2012) of framewise dis- placement and DVARS with removal of volumes before and after a root-mean-square displace
evidence_spans.claim: Motion was handled via framewise-displacement/DVARS-based scrubbing of individual volumes.

evidence_spans.text: Overall, a leave-one-out classiﬁer was used to generate a classiﬁcation score for each of the 964 subjects, leaving out one subject at a time and calculating the classiﬁcation score for the left out sub- ject.
evidence_spans.claim: Evaluation used a leave-one-subject-out classifier across all 964 subjects.

evidence_spans.text: Age, age-squared, gender, handedness, and site were included as covariates for the classiﬁer.
evidence_spans.claim: Site was included as a covariate adjusted for in the classifier.

evidence_spans.text: As high as 60% accuracy was obtained for whole brain classiﬁcation, with the best accuracy from connections involving regions of the default mode network, parahippocampaland fusiform gyri, insula, Wernicke Area, and intraparietal sulcus.
evidence_spans.claim: Best whole-brain classification accuracy was 60%, driven by default-mode, parahippocampal/fusiform, insula, Wernicke and intraparietal-sulcus connections.

evidence_spans.text: Multisite functional connectivity classiﬁcation of autism outperformed chance using a simple leave-one-out classiﬁer, but exhibited poorer accuracy than for single site results.
evidence_spans.claim: Multisite classification outperformed chance but underperformed prior single-site classification results.

assessments.support: 964 of 1112 ABIDE I subjects (447 autism/517 TD) from 16 sites retained after explicit preprocessing-success inclusion criteria (Table with demographics, ADI-R/ADOS/IQ reported).
Custom SPM8 pipeline fully specified step-by-step (slice timing, realignment, coregistration, normalization, nuisance regression, motion scrubbing) with a 7266-ROI gray-matter lattice.
Diagnosis source given as the ABIDE phenotypic file with reported ADI-R, ADOS, and IQ instrument scores for subgroups.

Leave-one-out classifier with age/sex/handedness/site covariates is well described, but it is not stated whether connection selection (t-test-based binning) was recomputed excluding the left-out subject at every iteration or on a dataset including that subject.

risk_of_bias.summary: A methodologically transparent, large multisite ABIDE I replication attempt; the main appraisal uncertainty is whether per-connection statistical selection was leakage-free within the leave-one-out loop.

narrative_row.methods: Custom SPM8 preprocessing pipeline; whole-brain functional connectivity over a 7266-ROI gray-matter lattice; leave-one-subject-out classifier with age, age-squared, gender, handedness and site as covariates
narrative_row.outcomes: Maximum 60% whole-brain classification accuracy, above chance but below the ~80% previously reported for single-site classification; most discriminative connections involved default mode network, parahippocampal/fusiform gyri, insula, Wernicke area, and intraparietal sulcus; classifier score correlated with symptom severity, social function, daily living skills and verbal IQ

charting.authors: Ktena SI; Parisot S; Ferrante E; Rajchl M; Lee M; Glocker B; Rueckert D

evidence_spans.claim: Head-motion parameters were estimated via SPM8 realignment (6 rigid-body parameters) rather than a connectivity pipeline.

assessments.support: Explicit site-level inclusion rules (raw uncorrected scans, >=8 min scan duration, >=15 ASD individuals), yielding 7 of 16 ABIDE sites and 605 participants (304 ASD, 301 CT).
Per-site N by diagnosis reported (e.g. UM_1: NASD=55, NCT=55); age groups, comorbidity and medication-class tables reported.
SPM8 realignment-based estimation of 6 rigid-body motion parameters fully described as the analysis 'pipeline' (since motion itself, not BOLD connectivity, is the outcome).
ASD/CT group membership drawn from the ABIDE phenotypic file; ADOS mentioned as available but the paper does not restate the diagnostic criteria used to assign ASD status.
Age-group stratification (G1-G5), site-level breakdowns, comorbidity and medication class are all explicitly examined as potential confounders/modifiers.
Separate analyses performed by site, age group, medication status (naive vs. 2+ vs. 3+ medications) and comorbidity status rather than pooling uncritically.
Outcome is a validated stochastic (Gamma-distribution noise-to-signal ratio) characterisation of micro-movement waveforms, methodologically detailed.

Non-parametric distributional analyses (K-S tests) and confidence-interval comparisons are used extensively, but explicit correction for the large number of site x age x medication subgroup comparisons is not clearly described.

risk_of_bias.summary: A methodologically unusual but well-specified associational ABIDE study that repurposes raw resting-state fMRI head-motion time series as the outcome of interest, with explicit site-level inclusion criteria and per-site/per-subgroup N, though diagnostic-instrument detail and multiple-comparisons correction are less explicit.

charting.reviewer_notes: A secondary 130-subject adult ABIDE I subsample (63 ASD, 67 NT, ages 18-50) was used only to assess generalization of the framework, not as the primary analysed cohort.

narrative_row.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction; ABIDE I; 452 adolescents (201 ASD, 251 neurotypical) from 17 sites (primary sample), plus a 130-subject adult generalization subsample (63 ASD, 67 NT)
narrative_row.methods: C-PAC-preprocessed rs-fMRI BOLD signals over AAL90 ROIs combined with an anatomical k-nearest-neighbor brain graph; Graph Signal Processing (extended Fukunaga-Koontz transform) features classified via an interpretable decision tree; Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation with inner CV for hyperparameter tuning
narrative_row.outcomes: Averaged test accuracy up to 74.8% (m=3), significantly outperforming a structural-only (SFM) baseline and a functional-only (GFT) baseline; predictive markers implicate frontal and temporal lobe regions; framework also generalizes to an independent adult subsample with up to a 15-point accuracy gap over SFM
narrative_row.key_limitations: No leave-site-out evaluation despite 17-site heterogeneity; diagnostic-instrument source not restated; 'structural' network is an anatomical-distance graph rather than a diffusion-derived structural connectome
narrative_row.relevance_notes: Demonstrates that combining a geometric/anatomical brain graph with rs-fMRI graph-signal features improves interpretable ASD classification over single-modality baselines on a well-specified ABIDE I adolescent subset

kg_link.cohort_description: 452 ABIDE I adolescent participants (201 ASD, 251 neurotypical) from 17 sites, selected for eyes-open acquisition, age under 18, and mean framewise displacement under 0.2mm; a secondary 130-subject adult subsample (63 ASD, 67 NT) used for generalization
kg_link.pipeline: C-PAC (Preprocessed Connectomes Project)
kg_link.finding: A graph-signal-processing framework combining an anatomical brain graph with rs-fMRI BOLD signal frequency content achieves up to 74.8% averaged test accuracy classifying ASD vs. neurotypical participants, outperforming structural-only and functional-only baselines, with frontal and temporal lobe regions identified as most predictive.

evidence_spans.text:
we selected a 
subgroup of 190 subjects (102 with ASD and 88 TD) according to the following criteria: male 
children (age range: 6.5–13 years); rs-fMRI data acquired with open eyes; data from the 
University sites that provided the largest number of scans (KKI, NYU, UCLA, UM).
evidence_spans.claim: Cohort was a 190-subject (102 ASD, 88 TD) subset of ABIDE I selected by age, sex, eye status and site.

evidence_spans.text:
We analyzed the preprocessed data available on the ABIDE 
preprocessed homepage (29, 30), using the Configurable Pipeline 
for the Analysis of Connectomes (CPAC) (31), that includes slice-
timing, motion correction, intensity normalization, nuisance 
signal removal (e.g. tissue signals, low-frequency drifts), and 
registrations.
evidence_spans.claim: Preprocessing used the Preprocessed Connectomes Project CPAC pipeline.

evidence_spans.text:
Both anatomical and functional atlases were chosen to derive the 
FC measures; in particular, we chose Harvard-Oxford (HO) and 
Automatic Anatomical Labeling (AAL) as anatomical templates 
and Craddock-200 (CC) as functional templates to extract time 
series from brain regions
evidence_spans.claim: Four atlases (AAL, HO, CC, Power) were compared for the connectivity analysis.

evidence_spans.text:
a leave-site out cross-validation scheme was performed: 
each training set was composed by all the sites except one, that 
was left out for validation.
evidence_spans.claim: Classification used a leave-one-site-out cross-validation scheme.

evidence_spans.text:
The mean L-SVM classification performance, 
in terms of the area under the ROC curve (AUC), was 0.75 ± 0.05. The highest performance 
was obtained using data from KKI, NYU and UCLA sites in training and data from UM as testing 
set (AUC = 0.83).
evidence_spans.claim: Leave-one-site-out SVM classification reached mean AUC 0.75 ± 0.05, best fold AUC 0.83.

evidence_spans.text:
Specifically, stronger functional connectivity (FC) in ASD with respect to TD 
involve (p < 0.001) the angular gyrus with the precuneus in the right (R) hemisphere, and the 
R frontal operculum cortex with the pars opercularis of the left (L) inferior frontal gyrus.
evidence_spans.claim: ASD showed hyper-connectivity between right angular gyrus-precuneus (DMN) and right frontal operculum-left IFG pars opercularis.

evidence_spans.text:
implementation of the HO atlas. The binary classification 
results between subjects with ASD and controls in a leave-one-
site-out cross-validation scheme achieved an average accuracy 
of 0.71 ± 0.06 and an average AUC of 0.75  ± 0.05.
evidence_spans.claim: Best atlas (HO) gave leave-one-site-out accuracy 0.71 ± 0.06 and AUC 0.75 ± 0.05.

DATA AVAILABILITY
Publicly available datasets were analyzed in this study. This data 
can be found here: http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/abide/
evidence_spans.claim: Data availability statement points only to the general ABIDE repository, not a specific participant list for this subsample.

assessments.support: Explicit, stepwise selection criteria (age 6.5-13, male, eyes open, four most-populated sites) with resulting N by diagnosis given: "we selected a subgroup of 190 subjects (102 with ASD and 88 TD) according to the following criteria"
Named pipeline (CPAC) and four named atlases (AAL, HO, CC, Power) with feature counts per atlas reported in Table 4.
ASD/TD diagnosis is the ABIDE phenotypic diagnosis (DSM-5-based, ADOS Gotham scores reported), independent of the imaging predictor.

Leave-one-site-out cross-validation used throughout, whole-brain features without a tuned feature-selection step, and fixed default SVM hyperparameter to avoid a leakage-prone nested search: "a leave-site out cross-validation scheme was performed: each training set was composed by all the sites except one, that was left out for validation."

risk_of_bias.summary: Well-documented cohort-definition, pipeline, atlas choice and leave-one-site-out evaluation with no evident leakage; the main limitation is that only four of the larger ABIDE I sites are used and no held-out replication cohort is reported.

evidence_spans.text:
The rs-fMRI data used in this study were sourced from
the ABIDE I dataset, comprising 505 autistic individuals and
530 typical controls (TCs).
evidence_spans.claim: Dataset was ABIDE I with 505 ASD and 530 TC subjects.

evidence_spans.text:
The data is preprocessed using the Conﬁgurable Pipeline for
the Analysis of Connectomes (CPAC) pipeline, which includes
essential steps such as slice timing correction, voxel intensity
normalization, motion correction, nuisance signal removal, global
signal regression, band-pass ﬁltering, and spatial registration.
evidence_spans.claim: Preprocessing used the CPAC pipeline with standard steps including motion correction.

evidence_spans.text:
After preprocessing and quality control, the ﬁnal dataset consists
of 1,035 samples distributed as follows: 623 samples for the
training set, 308 samples for the validation set, and 104 samples
for the test set.
evidence_spans.claim: After QC, 1,035 subjects were split into a single train/validation/test partition (623/308/104), with no cross-validation or site handling described.

evidence_spans.text:
Functional connectivity matrices are derived from three brain
atlases (AAL, CC, EZ) using Pearson correlation coeﬃcients, which
are ﬂattened into one-dimensional vectors.
evidence_spans.claim: Features are Pearson-correlation connectivity matrices from three atlases (AAL, CC, EZ).

evidence_spans.text:
Results: The proposed model is evaluated using multiple ASD datasets. The
performance metrics include an average accuracy of 0.735, sensitivity of 0.765,
and speciﬁcity of 0.752, surpassing the results of existing state-of-the-art
methods.
evidence_spans.claim: Average performance across the three atlas-based datasets: accuracy 0.735, sensitivity 0.765, specificity 0.752.

evidence_spans.text:
our developed
MHOA based on the SSDAE model has accuracy 66.35%, 70.19%,
and 83.82% for EZ, AAL, and CC, respectively.
evidence_spans.claim: Per-atlas accuracy: EZ 66.35%, AAL 70.19%, CC 83.82%.

CPAC pipeline and three named atlases (AAL, CC, EZ) with Pearson-correlation connectivity matrices clearly described.

evidence_spans.text: The data used in the current study were provided by ABIDE I ( http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/abide/), and we use all 1102 subjects (ﬁlter_noglobal) processed by the Conﬁgurable Pipeline for the Analysis of Connectomes (CPAC) [22] for experiments.

evidence_spans.text:
We conduct experiments on all ABIDE I data (without any data screening), and obtain the mean 73.1%/73.4% accu-
racy on AAL/CC200 atlas
evidence_spans.claim: No data screening/QC exclusion was applied; the full 1102-subject ABIDE I release was used.

evidence_spans.text:
To validate the effectiveness of the proposed LRCDR
method, we conduct inter-site cross-validation experiments on
17 sites from ABIDE database. Speciﬁcally, one site is left
as the target domain for testing, and the remaining 16 sites
as multiple source domains for training.
evidence_spans.claim: Evaluation used leave-one-site-out inter-site cross-validation across all 17 ABIDE I sites.

evidence_spans.text:
The mean time series from 116 regions of interest (ROIs)
based on the automated anatomical labeling (AAL) atlas [23] are used for experiments.
evidence_spans.claim: Functional connectivity features used the AAL atlas (116 ROIs).

evidence_spans.text:
We also use the Craddock 200 (CC200) atlas [31] to
further verify the effectiveness of the LRCDR method and obtain the 73.4% mean accuracy.
evidence_spans.claim: CC200 atlas gave 73.4% mean leave-one-site-out accuracy.

evidence_spans.text:
For inter-site prediction on all ABIDE I data
(1102 subjects from 17 sites), LRCDR obtains the mean
accuracy of 73.1%, superior to the results of the compared
state-of-the-art domain adaptation methods and multi-site
ASD identiﬁcation methods.
evidence_spans.claim: LRCDR achieved 73.1% mean leave-one-site-out accuracy on AAL atlas, outperforming compared domain-adaptation methods.

evidence_spans.text:
In addition, we locate some
meaningful biomarkers: Most of the top important biomark-
ers are inter-network resting-state functional connectivi-
ties (RSFCs).
evidence_spans.claim: Feature-importance analysis identified mostly inter-network RSFCs as the most discriminative connections.

Pipeline (CPAC filter_noglobal) and two named atlases (AAL, CC200) with Pearson-correlation connectivity clearly described.

evidence_spans.text:
We limited ourselves to
acquisitions with repetition time of 2s (sites NYU, SDSU, UM, USM). This
resulted in a dataset of 147 subjects with ASD and 146 healthy controls.
evidence_spans.claim: Cohort restricted to four ABIDE sites with TR=2s: 147 ASD, 146 healthy controls.

evidence_spans.text:
The pre-processed acquisitions are
available as part of the Pre-processed Connectome Project (http://preprocessed- connectomes-project.org/abide/, C-PAC pipeline).
evidence_spans.claim: Data were preprocessed via the Preprocessed Connectomes Project, CPAC pipeline.

evidence_spans.text:
We
extracted rsfMRI time series using a 200-region parcellation CC200[?], estimated
subject-wise time-resolved connectivity matrices with windows lengths ranging
from 10 to 20 volumes (20-40s) and calculated node variability.
evidence_spans.claim: Dynamic functional connectivity was computed with sliding-window correlations over the CC200 atlas.

evidence_spans.text:
For inter-site, we employed a leave-
one-out-site approach that involved training the classiﬁer on all the sites
except the one left out for testing.
evidence_spans.claim: Inter-site evaluation used a leave-one-site-out approach.

evidence_spans.text:
Our analysis revealed that pa-
tients diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) show increased
FC variability in several brain regions that are associated with low FC
variability in the typical brain.
evidence_spans.claim: ASD patients showed increased dynamic FC variability in regions that are low-variability in typical controls.

evidence_spans.text:
We then used the enhanced FC variability
of brain regions as features for training machine learning models for ASD
classiﬁcation and achieved 65%
evidence_spans.claim: Node-variability features gave up to 65% classification accuracy.

evidence_spans.text:
Table 1 summarizes the performance of diﬀerent
classiﬁers on intra-site ASD prediction. The accuracy achieved by all classiﬁers
is comparable and is around 60%. The sensitivity varies between 60 to 65%. The
speciﬁcity is ˜60% for SVM and MLP, whereas RF and NB produce slightly lower
speciﬁcity.
evidence_spans.claim: Intra-site 5-fold CV: accuracy ~60%, sensitivity 60-65%, specificity ~60% (SVM, MLP).

evidence_spans.text:
The results on inter-site classiﬁcation are presented in Table 3. Whereas
the classiﬁcation accuracy using MLP is ˜62% for all sites, the speciﬁcity and
sensitivity vary across sites, consistent with the results shown in Figure 1b.
evidence_spans.claim: Leave-one-site-out classification accuracy using MLP was ~62% across sites.

assessments.support: N by diagnosis and site restriction (TR=2s sites only) are given, but no motion/QC exclusion rule beyond the TR filter is reported: "We limited ourselves to acquisitions with repetition time of 2s (sites NYU, SDSU, UM, USM). This resulted in a dataset of 147 subjects with ASD and 146 healthy controls."
CPAC pipeline and CC200 atlas with sliding-window dynamic connectivity clearly described.
ASD/control labels are the ABIDE phenotypic diagnosis, independent of the connectivity-derived predictors.

Both intra-site 5-fold cross-validation (pooled across sites) and a leave-one-site-out inter-site evaluation are reported; the intra-site pooled scenario does not control for site, but the leave-one-site-out scenario does, and no leakage-control statement is given for the node-selection step based on "a positive group-level diﬀerence across the three big sites (NYU, UM, and USM)" used to pick features.

screening.reason: Exclusion 3: uses only structural (T1-weighted) morphological MRI features from ABIDE (cortical thickness, surface area, volumes via FreeSurfer) for brain-age prediction; no resting-state functional MRI analysis is performed.

Exclusion 4 (no autism-vs-control analysis): this is primarily a statistical-methods paper (mixed-effects models for resampled network statistics) demonstrated on ABIDE UCLA and Michigan autism subjects only, relating ADOS symptom-severity covariates to connectivity density within the autism group. No autism-vs-typically-developing group-difference analysis or diagnostic classification is performed; the only mention of healthy subjects (n=90, Michigan) is used to construct a baseline network for a methods illustration/simulation, not as a compared control group.

Exclusion 4: ABIDE is used only as one of several unseen/generalizability test datasets (10 randomly selected, unlabeled images) to benchmark a deformable image registration network (FDRN); there is no autism-vs-control analysis and no diagnostic use of the data.
Meets inclusion 2/3: analyses ABIDE-I resting-state fMRI functional connectivity with a hierarchical graph-based deep-learning model (ASD-HNet) for ASD vs healthy-control classification.

evidence_spans.claim: Biomarker masks (A1-A20) were derived from FWE-corrected two-sample t-test group differences between ASD and TD in ABIDE, with explicit direction (A1-A10: ASD>TD; A11-A20: ASD<TD).

evidence_spans.text:
The results indicated that the biomarkers 
generated from the default mode and executive control networks significantly differed between the 
participants with ASD and TD. In particular, the biomarkers derived from the default mode network 
were negatively correlated with the raw scores and model factors of the SRS.
evidence_spans.claim: DMN- and executive-control-network-derived biomarkers differed between ASD and TD and correlated negatively with SRS severity scores.

evidence_spans.text:
The results of this study indicate that the FC of DMN in the ASD group was 
weaker than that of the TD group.
evidence_spans.claim: DMN functional connectivity was weaker (hypoconnectivity) in ASD than TD.

evidence_spans.text:
The areas 
under the curve (AUCs) for the biomarkers were (0.590, 0.745, p < 0.05), (0.588, 0.646), and (0.646, 0.677) for 
(R4, A4), (R5, A15), and (R8, A18), respectively.
evidence_spans.claim: ROC analysis on the local cohort gave AUCs up to 0.745 (A4, DMN-derived biomarker), significantly higher than its R-template counterpart.

evidence_spans.text:
The pipelines, as well as the 30 masks of this study, are available28. The 
open-science materials and tools, including the RSN10 template, C-PAC, ABIDE, and our pipeline, can be used 
to replicate the methods of this study.
evidence_spans.claim: The 30 biomarker masks (not the local participant data) are shared publicly, aiding methodological but not full cohort reproducibility.

FWE-corrected two-sample t-tests (FSL-randomise, 5000 permutations) for group differences, and FDR-adjusted p-values for the SRS/SNAP correlation analysis.

evidence_spans.text: DSM-IV-TR diagnosed Asperger’s disorder (n = 79), pervasive developmental disorder-not otherwise specified [PDD-NOS] (n = 58) and Autistic disorder (n = 92) from ABIDE II were used as discovery cohort, and ABIDE I (n = 400) was used for replication.

evidence_spans.text: Subjects with ASD (n = 229) and the corresponding TDCs (n = 126) were selected from the ABIDE II [29, 30], which is hosted by the 1000 Functional Connectome Project/International Neuroimaging Data-sharing Ini- tiative (INDI) from multiple international sites (9 sites, Additional file 1: Table S1).
evidence_spans.claim: ABIDE II discovery sample: 229 ASD, 126 TDC from 9 sites.

evidence_spans.text: we removed outlier datasets with mean FD exceeding 1 mm, as well as head motion exceeding 2.0 mm of maximal translation (in any direction of x, y or z) or 1.0° of maximal rotation through- out the course of scanning.
evidence_spans.claim: Motion QC excluded scans with mean FD>1mm or motion >2.0mm/1.0 degree.

evidence_spans.text: to calculate fALFF [34], the sum of the spectral amplitude values in the 0.01–0.08 Hz low-frequency power range was divided by the sum of the amplitudes over the entire detectable power spectrum (range: 0–0.25 Hz).
evidence_spans.claim: fALFF computed as ratio of low-frequency (0.01-0.08Hz) spectral power to total power (0-0.25Hz).

evidence_spans.text: the preprocessed multimodal MRI features were jointly analyzed by a fusion-with-reference model called “MCCAR + jICA”

charting.title: Evaluation of Augmentation Methods in Classifying Autism Spectrum Disorders from fMRI Data with 3D Convolutional Neural Networks
charting.primary_goal: Evaluate how different data-augmentation strategies affect 3D-CNN test accuracy for classifying ASD vs controls from ABIDE resting-state fMRI ReHo derivatives.
charting.study_setting: Multi-site (ABIDE I, 17 sites per the full release)
charting.specific_features: ReHo derivative volumes (no ROI atlas; voxel-wise 3D CNN input)
charting.feature_extraction_tools: CCS (Connectome Computation System) via ABIDE preprocessed
charting.model_category: Deep learning (3D CNN)
charting.specific_algorithms: 3D CNN (3 convolutional layers + dense layer + sigmoid output) trained with various data-augmentation strategies (scaling, rotation, brightness, elastic deformation)
charting.validation_methodology: 70/15/15 train/validation/test split, 10-fold cross-validation for mean test accuracy
charting.performance_metrics: Test accuracy (10-fold CV mean and SD)
charting.key_performance_results: Compared to no augmentation, the best augmentation approach increases the test accuracy by 0.6 percentage units. elastic deformations seem to work best, with an improvement of 2.2 percentage units.
charting.summary_key_findings: Data augmentation provided only minor improvements in 3D-CNN test accuracy for ASD-vs-control classification on ABIDE ReHo data (0.6-2.2 percentage points depending on strategy and stopping criterion); about half of the augmentation strategies tested reduced test accuracy relative to no augmentation, and training accuracy well above 90% indicated overfitting.
charting.future_directions_recommended: Evaluate other ABIDE-preprocessed derivatives and multi-channel 3D CNNs combining several derivatives.

charting.title: CNNG: A Convolutional Neural Networks With Gated Recurrent Units for Autism Spectrum Disorder Classification
charting.primary_goal: Classify ASD vs. typical controls directly from 4D spatio-temporal resting-state fMRI using a joint 3D-CNN + GRU (CNNG) deep-learning model.
charting.feature_types: Raw 4D spatio-temporal fMRI volumes (downsampled, voxel-wise, no ROI/atlas)
charting.specific_features: 28x28x28 spatial volumes x 32 timepoints, fed directly into a 3D-CNN+GRU network

charting.model_category: Deep learning (3D CNN + Gated Recurrent Unit)
charting.specific_algorithms: CNNG: stacked small 3D convolutional kernels (3x3x3) for spatial features + GRU for temporal features, compared against LSTM variant, CNN-MLP, DiagNet, HI-GCN, GAT, SVC
charting.validation_methodology: Single 8:2 train/test split (no cross-validation reported for the main result); per-site average accuracy/sensitivity/specificity also reported across the 17 sites
charting.key_performance_results: the proposed algorithm obtains an accuracy of 72.46% in the experiment of 871 subjects, which is 5.26% higher than that of HI-GCN, 4.44% higher than that of GAT, and 2.44% higher than that of CNN. The proposed algorithm also obtains a speciﬁcity of 79.25% and a sensitivity of 74.35%. the AUC value of the proposed algorithm is 0.79, which is 5.42% higher compared to GAT.
charting.summary_key_findings: CNNG achieved 72.46% accuracy, 74.35% sensitivity, 79.25% specificity and AUC 0.79 for ASD vs TC classification from raw spatio-temporal ABIDE-I fMRI, outperforming CNN-MLP, DiagNet, HI-GCN and GAT comparators.

screening.reason: Analyses ABIDE-I resting-state functional connectivity (vertex-wise, C-PAC pipeline) for a group-difference (ASD vs NT) analysis; meets inclusion 2-3.

evidence_spans.text: We studied 211 males from three sites of the ABIDE-I dataset comprising 103 participants with an ASD diagnosis (mean ± SD age = 20.8 ± 8.1 years) and 108 neurotypical controls (NT, 19.2 ± 7.2 years).
evidence_spans.claim: Cohort was 211 males (103 ASD, 108 NT) from three ABIDE-I sites.

evidence_spans.text: Compared to NT, ASD participants presented with widespread reductions in CD, generally indicating shorter average connection length and thus suggesting reduced long-range connectivity but increased short-range connections.
evidence_spans.claim: Main finding: ASD shows widespread connectivity-distance reductions, implying relatively reduced long-range and increased short-range connectivity.

evidence_spans.text: included imaging and  clinical data from three different sites that included data  from > = 10 ASD and NT respectively, i.e., University of  Pittsburgh School of Medicine (PITT), New York Univer­ sity Langone Medical Center (NYU), and University of  Utah School of Medicine (USM).
evidence_spans.claim: Three ABIDE-I sites were used: PITT, NYU, USM.

evidence_spans.text: After excluding cases with high  head motion (cutoff: >2SD over mean framewise dis­ placement, n = 10), we obtained a sample size of n = 211  (103/108 ASD/NT).
evidence_spans.claim: A motion-based exclusion rule (>2 SD above mean FD) removed 10 subjects to reach n=211.

evidence_spans.text: based on  the configurable pipeline for the analysis of connectomes  (C-PAC) (https://fcp-indi.github.io/) [83], including slice- time and head motion correction, skull stripping and  intensity normalization.
evidence_spans.claim: Preprocessing used the C-PAC pipeline.

evidence_spans.text: Subjects with a mean framewise displacement  (FD) > 0.3 mm in rs-fMRI (two SD from the mean across  all subjects) were excluded (n = 9).
evidence_spans.claim: An additional rs-fMRI-specific FD>0.3mm exclusion removed 9 subjects.

evidence_spans.text: Data were harmo­ nized for site effects while preserving effects of age and  ASD diagnosis using ComBat [86]
evidence_spans.claim: Site effects were handled using ComBat harmonization.

evidence_spans.text: Effect sizes dif­ fered across seven intrinsic functional networks [21],  with higher effects towards transmodal compared to  sensory/motor networks and peak reductions in CD in  the limbic network (Cohen's d=-0.159, Fig.  3A).
evidence_spans.claim: Peak effect size for CD reduction was in the limbic network (Cohen's d = -0.159).

assessments.support: Site, N, ADOS-based diagnosis and motion exclusion thresholds explicitly stated.
Table 1 gives age, IQ, ADOS by group; three named sites.
C-PAC pipeline with motion correction, CompCor, band-pass filter, no-GSR with GSR control analysis described in detail.
In-person diagnostic interview using ADOS described.
Age, head motion and site included as covariates/handled via ComBat; study restricted to males due to ABIDE-I female sparsity.
ComBat harmonization for site; motion exclusion thresholds applied; model CDi = ß0+ß1*Age+ß2*Diagnosis+ß3*Head Motion.
Connectivity distance derived from vertex-wise FC and geodesic distance mapping, a previously published approach.
Random field theory correction and FDR correction described for vertex-wise and cluster-wise tests.

risk_of_bias.summary: Well-documented cohort, pipeline, confound handling (ComBat, motion exclusion) and multiple-comparison correction for this associational analysis; main limitation is restriction to males and 3 of 17 ABIDE-I sites, explicitly acknowledged.

screening.reason: Analyses multi-site ABIDE resting-state fMRI functional connectivity and temporal entropy in an ASD-vs-control group-difference analysis; satisfies inclusion 2-3.

evidence_spans.text: Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) and structural imaging data of 85 individuals with ASD and 163 matched controls from multiple sites of the ABIDE data set (Di Martino et al., 2014) were included in this study for a total of N = 248 individuals.
evidence_spans.claim: Final analysed cohort: 85 ASD and 163 matched controls (N=248) from multiple ABIDE sites.

evidence_spans.text: Frames with excessive motion were identiﬁed and scrubbed  (Power et al., 2012) if the framewise displacement exceeded  0.3 mm. Individuals with >10% of their frames ﬂagged for  scrubbing were excluded.
evidence_spans.claim: Motion scrubbing threshold: FD>0.3mm flagged frames; individuals with >10% flagged frames excluded.

evidence_spans.text: ROIs were deﬁned as 10 mm diameter spheres whose center coordinates are given in MNI atlas space (Power et al., 2011).
evidence_spans.claim: Used the Power et al. (2011) 264-ROI functional atlas organized into 11 resting-state networks.

evidence_spans.text:
We observed that an imbalance in intra- and inter-network FC across 11 RSNs in ASD individuals (p = 0.002) corresponds to a weakened relationship with RSN
temporal entropy (p = 0.02).
evidence_spans.claim: Main finding: FC imbalance across 11 RSNs in ASD corresponds to a weaker FC-entropy relationship than in controls.

evidence_spans.text:
Further, we observed that an estimated RSN entropy model
signiﬁcantly distinguished ASD from controls (p = 0.01) and was associated with level of
ASD symptom severity (p = 0.003).
evidence_spans.claim: The entropy-model fit (not diagnosis-trained) significantly differed between ASD and control groups and correlated with ASD symptom severity.

evidence_spans.text: Importantly, no information about group membership (i.e., ASD or control) has been explicitly passed to the model.
evidence_spans.claim: The elastic-net entropy model was fit without using diagnostic group membership, i.e. it is an associational not a diagnostic-classification model.

evidence_spans.text:
The minimum MSE computed from a 10-fold cross validation
was 11.4 ± 7.2% of c1 variance, and was observed for α = 0.15.
evidence_spans.claim: Elastic-net model of FC from RSN entropy was fit with 10-fold cross-validation.

assessments.support: Explicit inclusion criteria (structural/functional scan requirements, full-scale IQ>100, FD threshold, minimum per-site N) stated.
Multi-site ABIDE cohort with per-site minimum (>=7 ASD and 7 control), demographic Table 1 referenced.
Detailed custom FSL-based pipeline (MCFLIRT, registration, scrubbing, band-pass filter, nuisance regression) fully described.
Refers to ABIDE site-specific diagnostic criteria rather than restating the diagnostic instrument directly.
Motion (FD) explicitly compared between groups and shown not significantly different (W=7,135, p=0.74); IQ>100 required as inclusion criterion.
Nuisance regression (motion, WM, CSF, global signal), scrubbing of high-motion frames, and explicit motion-equivalence check between groups.
FC (Power 264-ROI, 11 RSN) and wavelet-based entropy are both established and previously validated measures, cited and described in detail.

Wilcoxon rank-sum and multilinear regression with cross-validated elastic net are used, but explicit multiple-comparison correction across the many statistical tests reported is not detailed in the sections read.

risk_of_bias.summary: A methodologically careful multi-site ABIDE associational study with explicit motion thresholds, motion-equivalence testing between groups, and a diagnosis-blind entropy model later compared post hoc between groups.

charting.validation_methodology: 10-fold cross-validation (combined all-site dataset) and 5-fold cross-validation (site-wise)
charting.key_performance_results: Maximum 10-fold accuracy on combined 17-site dataset: 82% (Logistic Regression and Linear Discriminant classifiers, sensitivity 0.83, specificity 0.84-0.88); outperformed prior published methods (e.g. Heinsfeld et al. 2018: 63%; Taban Eslami et al. 2019: 67%) in the same comparison table; outperformed state-of-the-art in 13 of 17 individual sites using 5-fold CV
charting.summary_key_findings: On the full preprocessed ABIDE-I dataset (17 sites, 505 ASD/530 controls after removing subjects with missing information), a novel 3-stage Teacher-Student-and-SFFS feature selection approach on 90x90 AAL-atlas connectivity matrices achieved a maximum 10-fold cross-validated accuracy of 82% on the combined dataset (Logistic Regression/Linear Discriminant classifiers) and outperformed prior state-of-the-art methods in 13 of 17 individual sites.
charting.reviewer_notes: Feature-ranking (Teacher-Student) and feature-selection (SFFS) steps appear to precede the reported cross-validation rather than being nested within folds, a potential leakage concern not explicitly addressed in the text read.

narrative_row.study_design_sample_dataset: Diagnostic prediction; ABIDE-I, all 17 sites; n=505 ASD / 530 controls (N=1035) after removing subjects with missing information.
narrative_row.methods: C-PAC-preprocessed data; AAL atlas (90 regions, 90x90 FC matrix); novel Teacher-Student deep-learning feature ranking plus Sequential Forward Feature Selection (SFFS); classifiers (LR, LD, SVM, RF, DT) evaluated with 10-fold (combined) and 5-fold (site-wise) cross-validation.
narrative_row.outcomes: Maximum 82% 10-fold accuracy on the combined 17-site dataset (LR/LD), outperforming prior published ABIDE classifiers in the same comparison table, and outperforming state-of-the-art in 13/17 individual sites.
narrative_row.key_limitations: Feature selection (Teacher-Student + SFFS) appears performed prior to, rather than nested within, the reported cross-validation folds (potential leakage); all 17 sites pooled with explicitly ignored site variability and no leave-site-out evaluation; no motion/QC threshold or code/data release reported.
narrative_row.relevance_notes: A full-ABIDE-I (17-site) classification benchmark illustrating a novel feature-selection method, useful for the knowledge graph's predictive-methods comparisons but with notable risk-of-bias caveats around leakage and site pooling.
